Decoding reads every weight at every step, so a weight stored in fewer bytes is read sooner. In the memory-bound regime the gain is direct: half the bytes, up to twice the tokens per second. Quantization also frees memory for the cache, and on large models that is often the bigger win:

Llama 3.1 70B in 16 bits barely fits on two H100s. With 90% of their memory given to the engine, vLLM’s default, there is room for 41,000 tokens of cache: five conversations of 8K. In 8 bits, the same two GPUs hold six times more cache and double the ceiling for one sequence.

In 4 bits the model fits on one GPU with room for 128,000 tokens. The bars leave out the engine’s memory for activations and the scales that quantized formats store, so real numbers are somewhat lower.

The methods differ in what they quantize:

  • Weights only. Weights are stored in 4 or 8 bits and multiplied in 16. GPTQ chooses how to round each weight using second-order information and quantizes a 175B model in about four GPU hours. AWQ observes that “protecting only 1% salient weights can greatly reduce quantization error”, finds those weights from activation statistics, and protects them by scaling rather than by keeping them in higher precision. Weight-only formats speed up memory-bound decoding. At large batches, where the step is compute-bound, unpacking the weights is extra work, and they can be slower than 16 bits.
  • Weights and activations. With both in 8 bits, the GPU’s 8-bit arithmetic does the multiplication too. LLM.int8() showed why this is hard: from about 6.7B parameters, a few hidden dimensions carry values far larger than all the others, in every layer. The method keeps those dimensions in 16 bits and multiplies the rest, more than 99.9% of the values, in 8. On H100s, FP8 doubles the dense tensor throughput, from 989 to 1,979 TFLOPS, so the prefill gets faster as well.
  • The KV cache. Stored in 8 bits, it takes half the memory, and twice the context or twice the batch fits.

How much quality a format costs depends on the model, the method and the task. Measure it on your own task, before and after: an average over general text, such as perplexity, can hide losses in exactly the cases you care about, such as arithmetic, code or a less common language.

Guessing ahead: speculative decoding

The roofline has a strange gift. A decoding step reads all the weights to produce one token, and reading them to check five tokens costs about the same, because the step is memory-bound either way. Speculative decoding[2, 3] makes use of it.

A small draft model, cheap to run, proposes \(\gamma\) tokens one by one. The large target model reads all of them in a single forward pass, which gives its own prediction at every position.

The proposals are accepted up to the first one the target disagrees with, and there the target’s own token is taken instead. Every round yields at least one token and at most \(\gamma + 1\).

Here is a real round. Qwen2.5-0.5B drafts for Qwen2.5-1.5B, and both take their most likely token:

With greedy decoding, acceptance means that both models choose the same token, and the text is exactly what the target would write alone. I checked: the 200 tokens produced this way are identical to plain greedy decoding with the target.

With sampling, the papers accept each proposal with probability \(\min\left(1, p(x)/q(x)\right)\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are the target’s and the draft’s probabilities of the proposed token, and on rejection they sample from what is left of \(p\). The output then follows the target’s distribution exactly, “within hardware numerics”, as Chen et al. put it.

How many tokens does a round give? If each proposal is accepted with probability \(\alpha\), independently of the others, the expected number of tokens per pass of the target is (Leviathan et al., equation 1)

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{tokens}] = \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma + 1}}{1 - \alpha} .\]

Read it as a sum. One token is certain. A second comes if the first proposal is accepted, with probability \(\alpha\); a third if the first two are, \(\alpha^2\); and so on up to \(\alpha^\gamma\).

The formula is this geometric series added up. Even a perfect draft gives no more than \(\gamma + 1\) tokens, and a weak one no more than \(1/(1-\alpha)\), however far ahead it guesses.

On a 200-token answer the 0.5B draft and the 1.5B target agreed often enough for \(\alpha = 0.75\), estimated from how many proposals each round accepted. The formula then predicts 3.29 tokens per pass, and the measured 3.23 is close:

Tokens per pass are not yet speed. The draft runs \(\gamma\) times per round, and if a draft pass costs a fraction \(c\) of a target pass, the expected speedup is (Leviathan et al., theorem 3.8)

\[\text{speedup} = \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma + 1}}{(1 - \alpha)(\gamma c + 1)} .\]

Our pair is badly matched for it. Decoding is memory-bound, so a pass costs about in proportion to the parameters it reads: \(c \approx 0.49 / 1.54 = 0.32\), and with \(\gamma = 5\) the speedup is \(3.29 / 2.6 \approx 1.26\).

A draft a hundredth of the target’s size would give 3.1 with the same \(\alpha\); in Leviathan et al.’s experiments, drafts about two orders of magnitude smaller than the target usually did best.

In practice the draft often isn’t a separate model at all. Medusa and EAGLE attach small extra heads to the target itself that predict further ahead; n-gram lookup drafts by copying from the prompt, which works when the answer quotes it, as in code editing.

DeepSeek-V3 trains a module that predicts one more token alongside the model, and its report gives an acceptance rate of 85 to 90% for that token and 1.8 times the tokens per second.

The gift has a condition. Checking \(\gamma\) tokens is nearly free only while the step is memory-bound.

At large batches the GPU is already busy computing, the extra positions cost real time, and the speedup shrinks or turns into a slowdown. Speculative decoding buys latency when the load is light; measure it under the load you actually have.

Attention kernels

The prefill computes attention between every pair of prompt tokens. Written plainly, attention puts the score matrix, \(T \times T\) for every head, into GPU memory, and reads it back for the softmax and again for the weighted sum of values.

FlashAttention computes the same result in tiles that fit in the on-chip SRAM and never writes the full matrix out. It is exact, not an approximation, and its authors measured attention 7.6 times faster on GPT-2.

The quadratic part is visible on the T4: an 8,192-token prompt took 9.9 s to read, 4.2 times as long as 4,096 tokens, so at that length attention, not the weights, sets the time.

Decoding has one query per sequence and no large matrix to avoid; its cost is reading the cache, as the measurement above showed. What matters is how many of the GPU’s cores share that reading.

A kernel that gives each sequence and head to one block of threads leaves most of the GPU idle when the batch is small and the context is long.

Flash-Decoding also splits the cache along its length, computes attention over the pieces in parallel and combines them using each piece’s log-sum-exp, for “up to 8x faster generation for very long sequences”.

The kernel matters even for this simple job: on the T4, a fused attention kernel read the cache at about 200 GB/s, and the same attention written as two matrix products and a softmax at 91 GB/s.

More than one GPU

When the weights don’t fit on one GPU, or one GPU decodes too slowly, the model is split. Inside one server the usual way is tensor parallelism, as in Megatron-LM: every GPU holds a slice of every weight matrix.

The attention heads are divided among the GPUs, and so is the MLP: its first matrix by columns, its second by rows. Each GPU then holds a partial sum of the block’s output, and an all-reduce adds the parts up, twice per layer in the forward pass.

Each GPU reads only its share of the weights, so their bandwidths add up, and two H100s decode Llama 3.1 70B about twice as fast as one would if the model fit.

The all-reduces are the price. Llama 3.1 70B makes 160 of them for every generated token, and at each one all GPUs wait for the slowest. The messages are small, 8,192 numbers per sequence, so the link’s latency matters as much as its bandwidth:

link bandwidth per direction
NVLink, H100 450 GB/s
NVLink, A100 300 GB/s
PCIe 5.0 x16 64 GB/s
PCIe 4.0 x16 32 GB/s
InfiniBand NDR, one port 50 GB/s (400 Gb/s)

NVIDIA quotes NVLink as the sum of both directions: 900 GB/s for H100 and 600 for A100. Tensor parallelism stays inside a server, on NVLink.

Across servers the model is split by layers instead, pipeline parallelism: each group of GPUs runs a range of layers and passes the activations on once per step. It needs far less communication, but a stage stands idle unless several batches are in flight at once.

Mixture-of-experts models add expert parallelism: DeepSeek-V3 sends every token to 8 of its 256 routed experts in each MoE layer, and the experts live on different GPUs.

The system around the engine

The engine is one box on a longer path, and every box on it can undo the engine’s work.

Streaming. Tokens go back to the client as they are generated, usually as server-sent events on one long HTTP response. Any hop that buffers the response turns the stream into a few bursts.

The classic one is nginx, which buffers proxied responses by default. Turn buffering off for the streaming location, or send X-Accel-Buffering: no from the application[4]:

location /v1/ {
    proxy_pass http://engine:8000;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;  # the default 60 s can run out before the first token
}

If tokens still arrive in clumps, look lower. Nagle’s algorithm holds a small write until the previous one is acknowledged, and Linux delays acknowledgements by 40 to 200 ms; a server turns Nagle off on the socket with TCP_NODELAY.

Queues and backpressure. Little’s law tells how many requests are inside at a given rate. When requests arrive faster than the GPUs serve them, the queue grows without limit, and everyone in it eventually times out after the longest possible wait.

A bounded queue with fast rejection is kinder: answer 429 with a Retry-After header when the expected wait exceeds what the client will tolerate, and let the client retry or fall back.

Count tokens as well as requests, since a request with a 100,000-token prompt takes as much of the engine’s time as a hundred requests of a thousand tokens, or more. And when a client disconnects, abort its request in the engine, or the GPU keeps generating tokens that nobody reads.

Scaling. GPU utilization is the wrong signal for autoscaling: as the first chart showed, it says 100% for a single sequence. Scale on what users feel and on what limits the batch: requests waiting, KV cache usage, TTFT.

A new replica is slow to start. Llama 3.1 70B in bf16 is 141 GB; at 1 GB/s from network storage, reading it takes more than two minutes, before the engine has captured its CUDA graphs and warmed up.

Keep the weights close to the GPUs, keep a warm replica in reserve, and scale out when the queue starts to grow, not when it is already long.

What to watch. vLLM exports the essentials as Prometheus metrics[1]: vllm:num_requests_waiting and vllm:num_requests_running, vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc, vllm:num_preemptions, vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds, vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds, and vllm:prefix_cache_hits against vllm:prefix_cache_queries.

Watch TTFT and time per token separately, and at the 99th percentile as well as the median: a chunked-prefill budget that is too large shows up as a long tail in time per token while the median looks fine.

For every request, log the time in the queue, in prefill and in decoding, and the number of input and output tokens.

References

  1. vLLM: automatic prefix caching, preemption, metrics. ↩
  2. Leviathan et al. Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding. ICML 2023. ↩
  3. Chen et al. Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling. 2023. ↩
  4. nginx: proxy_buffering. ↩
  5. Kwon et al. Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention. SOSP 2023.
  6. Yu et al. Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models. OSDI 2022.
  7. Agrawal et al. Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve. OSDI 2024.
  8. Zhong et al. DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving. OSDI 2024.
  9. Zheng et al. SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs. 2023.
  10. Shazeer. Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need. 2019.
  11. Ainslie et al. GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints. EMNLP 2023.
  12. DeepSeek-AI. DeepSeek-V2, 2024, and DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report, 2024.
  13. Frantar et al. GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers. ICLR 2023.
  14. Lin et al. AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration. MLSys 2024.
  15. Dettmers et al. LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale. NeurIPS 2022.
  16. Cai et al. Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads. 2024.
  17. Li et al. EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty. 2024.
  18. Dao et al. FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness. NeurIPS 2022.
  19. Dao et al. Flash-Decoding for long-context inference. 2023.
  20. Shoeybi et al. Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism. 2019.
  21. NVIDIA: nvidia-smi, DCGM profiling metrics, datasheets of the T4, A100 and H100.
  22. Anthropic: API pricing.

The measurements: experiment.py (Kaggle T4), speculative.py (CPU), and the figures, figures.py, with the data they were drawn from.
entry.summary: Where the time and the memory go when a language model serves users, measured on a real GPU, and what serving engines do about it

entry.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: Adapters, LoRA and the Rest, in PyTorch

link.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: Adapters, LoRA and the Rest, in PyTorch

entry.content:
In 2020 Armen Aghajanyan, Luke Zettlemoyer and Sonal Gupta fine-tuned RoBERTa-Large, a model with 355 million parameters, by training about 200 numbers. They chose a random 200-dimensional subspace of the full parameter space, let the optimizer move only inside it, and reached 90% of what full fine-tuning gets on MRPC, a paraphrase task[1].

Larger models needed even smaller subspaces. Two years later Tim Dettmers and colleagues fine-tuned a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU, in 24 hours, and got a chatbot that GPT-4, acting as judge, rated at 99.3% of ChatGPT; the authors themselves warn that such benchmarks have wide error bars[2].

Both results say the same thing: adapting a pretrained model to a task changes very little of it. (If the transformer itself needs a refresher, the course Transformers: from scratch to production builds one.)

Most of what the model knows stays put, and the change that matters can be written down with a tiny number of parameters. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is the family of methods built on that observation.

This post goes through the main ones: what each adds to a transformer, written in a few lines of PyTorch, and how they compare when trained on the same task with the same budget.

What full fine-tuning costs

Fine-tuning every weight is the reference everyone compares against, and it is expensive in two ways.

The first is memory during training. With the Adam optimizer in mixed precision, every parameter costs 16 bytes: 2 for the weight in 16 bits, 2 for its gradient, and 12 for the optimizer’s state, which keeps a 32-bit master copy of the weight and two running averages[3]. For an 8-billion-parameter model that is 128 GB before a single activation is stored:

Freeze the base model and train a few million parameters instead, and the gradients and optimizer state shrink to almost nothing: what remains is the weights themselves. Store those weights in 4 bits, as QLoRA does, and the 8B model trains in a few gigabytes.

The second cost is storage. Every fully fine-tuned version is a complete copy of the model. A hundred tasks mean a hundred copies; with PEFT they mean one base model and a hundred small files, often a few megabytes each, that can be loaded, swapped and combined at will.

One idea, many places to put it

Every method below follows the same recipe. Freeze the pretrained weights. Add, or select, a small set of parameters.

Train only those, together with a task head if there is one. Junxian He and colleagues showed that most PEFT methods can be written as one operation on a hidden state[4]:

\[h \leftarrow h + \Delta h ,\]

where \(h\) is some hidden representation inside the model and \(\Delta h\) is a small correction computed by the new parameters. That is the plain form; LoRA scales \(\Delta h\) by a constant, and prefix tuning, written this way, mixes \(h\) and \(\Delta h\) with a gate, \((1-\lambda) h + \lambda \Delta h\).

The methods differ in three choices: where \(\Delta h\) is added, what it is computed from, and how the function that computes it is parameterized. Keep those three questions in mind; each section below answers them for one method.

The survey by Vladislav Lialin and colleagues sorts the methods into families: those that add new parameters, those that select a subset of existing ones, and those that reparameterize the weight update[5]:

Figure 2 of Lialin, Deshpande, Yao and Rumshisky, "Scaling Down to Scale Up: A Guide to Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning" (version 2, 2024).

To compare the methods on equal terms, I wrote each of them in plain PyTorch, as small modules attached to a pretrained bert-base-uncased, and trained all of them on the same task: SST-2, deciding whether a sentence from a film review is positive or negative[6].

Every run uses the same 10,000 training sentences, three epochs, a learning rate chosen per method from its paper’s range, and three random seeds; every method also trains the classification head on top of BERT, about 592 thousand parameters.

The code is the code you will see below, and it ran on a Kaggle T4 (experiment.py).

Adapters

The first PEFT method for transformers, and still one of the most dependable, is the adapter of Neil Houlsby and colleagues[7]. Insert a small network into every layer, train only that network, leave everything else as it was.

The small network is a bottleneck: it projects the \(d\)-dimensional hidden state down to \(b \ll d\) numbers, applies a nonlinearity, projects back up, and adds the result to its input:

\[\text{Adapter}(h) = h + W_{\text{up}} \, \sigma\!\left(W_{\text{down}} h + b_{\text{down}}\right) + b_{\text{up}} ,\]

with \(W_{\text{down}}\) of shape \(b \times d\) and \(W_{\text{up}}\) of shape \(d \times b\). In bert-base \(d = 768\); with \(b = 64\) one adapter holds 99,136 parameters.

Two details decide whether this works. The first is the skip connection: the adapter computes a correction to \(h\), not a replacement for it. The second is the initialization.

If \(W_{\text{up}}\) starts at zero, the adapter’s output is exactly \(h\), so at the first step of training the model computes exactly what the pretrained model computed, and the optimizer starts from there.

Houlsby et al. initialize near the identity for this reason, and warn that “if the initialization deviates too far from the identity function, the model may fail to train.” Start from random weights instead, and every layer’s output is distorted before training even begins.

class Adapter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, bottleneck):
        super().__init__()
        self.down = nn.Linear(d, bottleneck)
        self.up = nn.Linear(bottleneck, d)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.up.weight)  # the adapter adds nothing until training moves it
        nn.init.zeros_(self.up.bias)

    def forward(self, h):
        return h + self.up(F.gelu(self.down(h)))

Where do adapters go? Houlsby et al. put two in every layer: after the projection that follows multi-head attention, and after the feed-forward block, in both cases before the residual connection and layer norm.

In Hugging Face’s BERT those projections are attention.output.dense and output.dense, and the cleanest way to insert an adapter is to replace each projection with “the projection, then the adapter”:

def add_adapters(model, bottleneck=64):
    for layer in model.bert.encoder.layer:
        # after attention and after the feed-forward block, before the residual and the layer norm
        for sub in (layer.attention.output, layer.output):
            sub.dense = nn.Sequential(sub.dense, Adapter(sub.dense.out_features, bottleneck))

Nothing else in the model changes: the residual addition and layer norm that follow dense still happen, now on the adapted output.

Houlsby et al. also trained the layer norms, and reported results “within 0.4% of the performance of full fine-tuning, adding only 3.6% parameters per task” on the GLUE benchmark.

Jonas Pfeiffer and colleagues later found that one adapter per layer, after the feed-forward block, performs on par “while … it requires only half the number of newly introduced adapters”[8]. Libraries long called the two layouts “Houlsby” and “Pfeiffer”.

Parallel adapters

A sequential adapter sits on the main path: every token’s hidden state must pass through it. He et al. moved it to the side. A parallel adapter reads the same input as the feed-forward block and adds its output, scaled by a constant \(s\), to the block’s output:

\[y = \text{FFN}(x) + s \cdot W_{\text{up}} \, \sigma(W_{\text{down}} x) .\]

In code this means rewriting BERT’s output module, which receives both the feed-forward hidden state and the block’s input x:

class ParallelFeedForward(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, output, bottleneck, scale=4.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.output = output  # BERT's: dense, dropout, LayerNorm(h + x)
        d = output.dense.out_features
        self.down = nn.Linear(d, bottleneck)
        self.up = nn.Linear(bottleneck, d)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.up.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.up.bias)
        self.scale = scale

    def forward(self, intermediate, x):
        h = self.output.dropout(self.output.dense(intermediate))
        h = h + self.scale * self.up(F.gelu(self.down(x)))
        return self.output.LayerNorm(h + x)

The two paths no longer depend on each other, so on hardware that runs them concurrently the adapter costs less extra time. He et al. found the parallel form at least as accurate as the sequential one, especially at the feed-forward block.

The scale \(s\) is a tuned hyperparameter; they used \(s = 4\) on summarization, and AdapterHub uses 4 as its default, as do we.

LoRA

Adapters add new computations to the model. LoRA, low-rank adaptation, adds none that survive training[9]. The linear algebra behind it has a post of its own; here is what it does inside a transformer. Its starting point is a hypothesis about the update itself.

Fine-tuning changes a weight matrix \(W\) to \(W + \Delta W\). LoRA assumes \(\Delta W\) has low rank: that it can be written as the product of a tall, thin matrix and a short, wide one,

\[W' = W + \Delta W = W + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A ,\]

where \(W\) is \(d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}\) and frozen, \(B\) is \(d_{\text{out}} \times r\), \(A\) is \(r \times d_{\text{in}}\), and the rank \(r\) is small, 8 for example. The constant \(\alpha / r\) scales the update so that changing \(r\) does not require retuning the learning rate.

A rank-\(r\) matrix maps every input into an \(r\)-dimensional subspace first (\(A x\)) and then out again (\(B\) times that). In words: LoRA lets fine-tuning change how the layer responds along a handful of directions, and nothing else. For a \(768 \times 768\) projection, the full update has 589,824 numbers and a rank-8 one has 12,288:

As with adapters, initialization makes the start harmless: \(A\) is random and \(B\) is zero, so \(BA = 0\) and the model begins exactly where the pretrained one was. The paper draws \(A\) from a Gaussian; Microsoft’s reference code and Hugging Face’s peft use Kaiming-uniform initialization, as below.

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base, r=8, alpha=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(r, base.in_features))
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(base.out_features, r))
        nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.A, a=math.sqrt(5))
        self.scale = alpha / r
        self.merged = False

    def forward(self, x):
        y = self.base(x)
        if not self.merged:
            y = y + (x @ self.A.T @ self.B.T) * self.scale
        return y

    @torch.no_grad()
    def merge(self):
        self.base.weight += self.scale * self.B @ self.A
        self.merged = True

Notice the order of operations in forward: x @ A.T first, then @ B.T. The input is squeezed to \(r\) numbers before it is expanded again, so the extra cost is two thin matrix products, never a full \(d \times d\) one.

The original paper applied LoRA to the query and value projections of attention, and so do we:

def add_lora(model, r=8, alpha=16, targets=("query", "value")):
    for layer in model.bert.encoder.layer:
        attention = layer.attention.self
        for name in targets:
            setattr(attention, name, LoRALinear(getattr(attention, name), r, alpha))

The merge method is LoRA’s best feature. After training, \(\frac{\alpha}{r} BA\) is just a matrix of the same shape as \(W\), so it can be added into \(W\) once, and the model is again an ordinary model: no extra layers, no extra latency.

In the experiment, merging changed the classifier’s outputs by at most \(2.1 \times 10^{-6}\), which is rounding error in 32-bit arithmetic.

Hu et al. report that on GPT-3 175B, LoRA cut the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and GPU memory during training by 3 times, from 1.2 TB to 350 GB, and that a task’s checkpoint shrank from 350 GB to 35 MB.

Is the update really low-rank?

LoRA’s hypothesis can be checked. After fully fine-tuning BERT in the experiment, I took the change in every query and value matrix, \(\Delta W = W_{\text{fine-tuned}} - W_{\text{pretrained}}\), and computed its singular values. The fraction of \(\|\Delta W\|^2\) captured by the top \(k\) singular directions tells how well a rank-\(k\) matrix could approximate the update:

The update is far from random. Its top 8 directions hold a median of 37% of it, against 4% for a random matrix of the same size. But it is not low-rank either: holding 90% of the update takes a median of 193 directions (from 28 to 228, depending on the matrix), against 392 for random noise.

Full fine-tuning spreads its change over many directions. LoRA does not work because that change is low-rank. It works because a rank-8 change turns out to be enough for the task, and the experiment below shows how close it gets.

Biderman et al. found the same on a much larger scale: full fine-tuning of Llama-2-7B made changes of a rank 10 to 100 times greater than the LoRA ranks people use.

QLoRA

QLoRA keeps LoRA’s adapters in 16 bits but stores the frozen base model in 4 bits[2]. The base weights are only read, never updated, so the quantization error enters the forward pass but not the optimizer.

Three ideas make it work: NF4, a 4-bit format whose levels are placed at the quantiles of a normal distribution, which suits trained weights; double quantization, which quantizes the scaling constants as well and saves about 0.37 bits per parameter; and paged optimizers, which use NVIDIA’s unified memory to move optimizer state to the CPU when a spike would otherwise run the GPU out of memory.

The paper also found that “LoRA on all linear transformer block layers are required to match full finetuning performance”, while the rank \(r\) mattered little.

(IA)³: rescaling instead of adding

The smallest addition that can still change a model’s behaviour is a multiplication. (IA)³, “Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations”, learns three vectors per layer and multiplies, element by element, the keys, the values and the hidden activations of the feed-forward block[10]:

\[\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q \, (l_k \odot K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) (l_v \odot V), \qquad (l_{ff} \odot \gamma(W_1 x)) \, W_2 .\]

Each vector starts at ones, which multiplies by one and changes nothing. Training moves each entry above one, amplifying a feature, or below, inhibiting it.

class Rescale(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, module, size):
        super().__init__()
        self.module = module
        self.scale = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(size))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.module(x) * self.scale


def add_ia3(model):
    for layer in model.bert.encoder.layer:
        attention = layer.attention.self
        attention.key = Rescale(attention.key, attention.key.out_features)  # l_k
        attention.value = Rescale(attention.value, attention.value.out_features)  # l_v
        hidden = layer.intermediate.dense.out_features
        layer.intermediate = Rescale(layer.intermediate, hidden)  # l_ff, after GELU

In bert-base that is \(768 + 768 + 3072 = 4{,}608\) numbers per layer, 55,296 in all, about 0.05% of the model. Like LoRA, the vectors can be folded into the weights after training, since \(l \odot (W x) = (l \odot W) x\).

BitFit: train the biases

BitFit adds nothing. It trains a subset of what is already there: the bias vectors of every linear layer and layer norm[11]. A bias shifts a layer’s output by the same vector for every token, so BitFit can move representations but cannot change how a layer mixes its inputs.

def bitfit(model):
    for name, p in model.bert.named_parameters():
        if name.endswith("bias"):
            p.requires_grad = True

There are 101,376 bias numbers in bert-base’s encoder, plus 768 in the embedding layer norm, under 0.1% of the model.

Prompt tuning and prefix tuning

The methods so far change what a layer computes. The next two change what it sees.

Prompt tuning prepends learned vectors to the input[12]. A text prompt is a sequence of token embeddings looked up in a table. A soft prompt is a sequence of embeddings that are parameters: the optimizer can place them anywhere in embedding space, not only at the positions of real words.

class SoftPrompt(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model, length=20):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = model
        vocabulary = model.get_input_embeddings().weight
        # begin from the embeddings of real words
        start = torch.randint(1000, vocabulary.shape[0], (length,))
        self.prompt = nn.Parameter(vocabulary[start].detach().clone())

    def forward(self, input_ids, attention_mask, labels=None):
        embeds = self.model.get_input_embeddings()(input_ids)
        prompt = self.prompt.expand(input_ids.shape[0], -1, -1)
        embeds = torch.cat([embeds[:, :1], prompt, embeds[:, 1:]], dim=1)
        mask = torch.cat([attention_mask[:, :1].expand(-1, prompt.shape[1]), attention_mask], dim=1)
        return self.model(inputs_embeds=embeds, attention_mask=mask, labels=labels)

The prompt goes after [CLS] because BERT classifies from the first position. Twenty vectors of 768 numbers are 15,360 parameters, by far the fewest of any method here, and the result shows it: in the experiment below it reached 85.5% on average, no better than training the classification head alone (85.9%).

Lester et al. found the same pattern on a much larger scale. With T5 models of up to 11 billion parameters, prompt tuning trailed full fine-tuning on small models and caught up with it only as models grew past a few billion parameters.

Prefix tuning gives the learned vectors more reach[13]. Instead of input embeddings, it learns keys and values for every layer: each layer’s attention sees \(p\) extra key-value pairs, as if \(p\) invisible tokens preceded the input at that depth:

\[\text{head} = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q \, [P_k ; K]^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) [P_v ; V] ,\]

where \([\,\cdot\,;\,\cdot\,]\) joins the learned rows \(P_k, P_v\) in front of the real keys and values. Queries still come only from the real tokens.

This is a change to attention itself, and recent versions of transformers let you register your own attention function under a name. The whole of prefix tuning is one such function, which joins the layer’s prefix in front of its keys and values and then calls the standard implementation:

def prefix_attention(module, query, key, value, attention_mask, **kwargs):
    batch = key.shape[0]
    # (batch, heads, length, head_dim), in the precision of the keys
    prefix_k = module.prefix_key.expand(batch, -1, -1, -1).to(key.dtype)
    prefix_v = module.prefix_value.expand(batch, -1, -1, -1).to(value.dtype)
    key = torch.cat([prefix_k, key], dim=2)
    value = torch.cat([prefix_v, value], dim=2)
    # the mask is boolean, True where attention is allowed: the prefix is always visible
    if attention_mask is not None:
        visible = attention_mask.new_ones(*attention_mask.shape[:-1], prefix_k.shape[2])
        attention_mask = torch.cat([visible, attention_mask], dim=-1)
    return sdpa_attention_forward(module, query, key, value, attention_mask, **kwargs)


AttentionInterface.register("prefix", prefix_attention)
AttentionMaskInterface.register("prefix", sdpa_mask)


def add_prefix(model, length=20):
    model.set_attn_implementation("prefix")
    for layer in model.bert.encoder.layer:
        attention = layer.attention.self
        shape = (1, attention.num_attention_heads, length, attention.attention_head_size)
        attention.prefix_key = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(shape) * 0.02)
        attention.prefix_value = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(shape) * 0.02)

The second registration matters: a custom attention function also needs a rule for building the padding mask, and without it the model silently passes no mask at all. Li and Liang trained the prefix through a small MLP rather than directly, because optimizing the raw vectors was unstable; after training the MLP is thrown away and only the prefix kept.

Compacter: adapters built from Kronecker products

Compacter shrinks the adapter’s two matrices further[14]. It builds each of them as a sum of Kronecker products. The Kronecker product \(A \otimes B\) of an \(m \times n\) matrix and a \(p \times q\) one is an \(mp \times nq\) matrix made of blocks: block \((i, j)\) is \(B\) multiplied by the entry \(a_{ij}\).

Compacter writes each adapter matrix as

\[W = \sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i \otimes B_i ,\]

with two twists that make it small. The \(n \times n\) matrices \(A_i\) are shared by every adapter in the model; they capture structure common to all layers. And each \(B_i\) has rank one, \(B_i = s_i t_i^\top\), so it costs only the length of two vectors.

With \(n = 4\), the down-projection of a 48-unit adapter in bert-base needs 816 numbers instead of 36,864. On T5-base the paper reports GLUE results on par with full fine-tuning while training 0.073% of the parameters, and 0.047% for Compacter++, which keeps only the adapter after the feed-forward block.

class PHMLinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, shared, d_in, d_out, zero=False):
        super().__init__()
        n = shared.shape[0]
        self.shared = shared  # (n, n, n): A_1 ... A_n, the same tensor in every layer
        if zero:
            self.s = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(n, d_out // n, 1))
        else:
            self.s = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n, d_out // n, 1) * 0.1)
        self.t = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n, 1, d_in // n) * 0.1)
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d_out))

    def weight(self):
        B = self.s @ self.t  # (n, d_out / n, d_in / n), each of rank one
        return sum(torch.kron(self.shared[i], B[i]) for i in range(len(B)))

    def forward(self, x):
        return F.linear(x, self.weight(), self.bias)

The adapter itself is unchanged; only its two nn.Linear layers become PHMLinear, with the up-projection’s \(s_i\) starting at zero so that, once again, the adapter starts as the identity.

The same task, ten ways

Here is how the methods compare on SST-2, against the number of parameters each trains besides the classification head:

method trained besides the head accuracy, % (3 seeds) time per run peak GPU memory
full fine-tuning all 109M 91.4 (91.2–91.9) 97 s 2.28 GiB
LoRA, q and v, r = 8 294,912 (0.27%) 90.9 (90.3–91.5) 48 s 1.26 GiB
adapters, sequential 2,379,264 (2.13%) 90.9 (90.5–91.3) 50 s 1.28 GiB
adapters, parallel 1,189,632 (1.07%) 90.8 (90.6–90.9) 45 s 1.19 GiB
BitFit 102,144 (0.09%) 90.2 (89.8–90.5) 44 s 1.20 GiB
Compacter 58,816 (0.05%) 90.0 (89.2–90.5) 110 s 1.25 GiB
(IA)³ 55,296 (0.05%) 89.6 (89.1–90.4) 55 s 1.44 GiB
prefix tuning 368,640 (0.34%) 88.3 (87.7–88.8) 44 s 1.22 GiB
task head only none 85.9 (84.7–86.7) 22 s 0.53 GiB
prompt tuning 15,360 (0.01%) 85.5 (84.7–86.0) 60 s 1.35 GiB

Three methods come within half a point of full fine-tuning: LoRA with 0.27% of the model’s parameters, and adapters in both arrangements with 1 to 2%.

BitFit, Compacter and (IA)³, each with less than a tenth of a percent, lose about one to two points. Prefix tuning loses three. Prompt tuning learned nothing that the task head alone did not, as Lester et al.’s results predict for a model this small.

The memory column shows a smaller saving than the chart at the top of this post, because bert-base is small: at 110 million parameters the activations of a batch take about as much memory as the optimizer state, and the activations remain.

Still, every method cut the peak memory of full fine-tuning by a third to a half, and most of them halved the time. Compacter is the exception in time: it rebuilds its matrices from Kronecker products at every step, which the other methods do not have to do.

A caution about reading too much into the ranking. This is one model, one task and three seeds, with learning rates taken from the papers rather than tuned for each method, and the ranges of the top four overlap. What the table shows reliably is the shape of the trade-off, not a winner.

In practice

Nobody writes these modules by hand for production. Hugging Face’s peft library implements most of them behind one interface:

from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification

model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased", num_labels=2)
config = LoraConfig(
    r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["query", "value"], lora_dropout=0.1, task_type="SEQ_CLS"
)
model = get_peft_model(model, config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
# ... train as usual, then:
model = model.merge_and_unload()  # LoRA folded into the weights; an ordinary model again

The adapters library from AdapterHub, which replaced the older adapter-transformers, does the same for bottleneck adapters, prefix tuning, Compacter and their combinations:

from adapters import AutoAdapterModel

model = AutoAdapterModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
# "seq_bn": one adapter per layer; "double_seq_bn": Houlsby's two; also "par_bn", "compacter", ...
model.add_adapter("sst2", config="seq_bn")
model.add_classification_head("sst2", num_labels=2)
model.train_adapter("sst2")  # freezes everything but the adapter and the head
# ... train, then keep only the adapter:
model.save_adapter("./sst2_adapter", "sst2")

A few things are worth knowing before you start:

  • Where to put LoRA. The original paper adapted the query and value projections. QLoRA found that adapting every linear layer of the blocks is what closes the gap with full fine-tuning, and peft accepts target_modules="all-linear" for that.
  • What LoRA does not learn. Dan Biderman and colleagues compared LoRA with full fine-tuning of Llama-2-7B on code and mathematics: in the usual low-rank settings LoRA learned less of the new domain and forgot less of the old one, and full fine-tuning made weight changes of “a rank that is 10-100× greater than typical LoRA configurations”[15]. For instruction tuning on a narrow task the trade is usually welcome; for teaching a model a new field through continued pre-training, it may not be.
  • Many adapters, one model. Because adapters are small and the base is shared, one server can hold many of them at once and apply a different one to each request. S-LoRA serves thousands of LoRA adapters on a single GPU[16], and vLLM applies adapters per request.

References

  1. Aghajanyan, A., Zettlemoyer, L., & Gupta, S. (2021). Intrinsic dimensionality explains the effectiveness of language model fine-tuning. ACL-IJCNLP. ↩
  2. Dettmers, T., Pagnoni, A., Holtzman, A., & Zettlemoyer, L. (2023). QLoRA: efficient finetuning of quantized LLMs. NeurIPS. ↩
  3. Rajbhandari, S., Rasley, J., Ruwase, O., & He, Y. (2020). ZeRO: memory optimizations toward training trillion parameter models. SC20. ↩
  4. He, J., Zhou, C., Ma, X., Berg-Kirkpatrick, T., & Neubig, G. (2022). Towards a unified view of parameter-efficient transfer learning. ICLR. ↩
  5. Lialin, V., Deshpande, V., Yao, X., & Rumshisky, A. (2023). Scaling down to scale up: a guide to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. arXiv:2303.15647. ↩
  6. Socher, R., et al. (2013). Recursive deep models for semantic compositionality over a sentiment treebank. EMNLP. ↩
  7. Houlsby, N., et al. (2019). Parameter-efficient transfer learning for NLP. ICML. ↩
  8. Pfeiffer, J., Kamath, A., Rücklé, A., Cho, K., & Gurevych, I. (2021). AdapterFusion: non-destructive task composition for transfer learning. EACL. ↩
  9. Hu, E. J., et al. (2021). LoRA: low-rank adaptation of large language models. ICLR 2022. ↩
  10. Liu, H., et al. (2022). Few-shot parameter-efficient fine-tuning is better and cheaper than in-context learning. NeurIPS. ↩
  11. Ben Zaken, E., Ravfogel, S., & Goldberg, Y. (2022). BitFit: simple parameter-efficient fine-tuning for transformer-based masked language-models. ACL. ↩
  12. Lester, B., Al-Rfou, R., & Constant, N. (2021). The power of scale for parameter-efficient prompt tuning. EMNLP. ↩
  13. Li, X. L., & Liang, P. (2021). Prefix-tuning: optimizing continuous prompts for generation. ACL-IJCNLP. ↩
  14. Karimi Mahabadi, R., Henderson, J., & Ruder, S. (2021). Compacter: efficient low-rank hypercomplex adapter layers. NeurIPS. ↩
  15. Biderman, D., et al. (2024). LoRA learns less and forgets less. TMLR. ↩
  16. Sheng, Y., et al. (2023). S-LoRA: serving thousands of concurrent LoRA adapters. MLSys 2024. ↩
  17. Libraries: Hugging Face peft, AdapterHub adapters, vLLM LoRA adapters.

The experiment, with every method above, and the figures: articles/adapters.
entry.summary: How to adapt a pretrained transformer by training a fraction of a percent of it: what adapters, LoRA, prefix and prompt tuning, BitFit, (IA)³ and Compacter add to the model, written out in PyTorch and measured on one task

entry.title: Is the Mind a Computer?
entry.content:
In 1950 Alan Turing made a prediction with numbers in it. In about fifty years, he wrote, computers would “play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 per cent chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning”[1].

He was a quarter of a century late, and then the machines overshot. In 2025 Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen ran Turing’s game as he described it: an interrogator chats for five minutes with two witnesses at once, one human and one machine, and has to say which is which.

Prompted to play “a young person who is introverted, knowledgeable about internet culture, and uses slang”, GPT-4.5 was picked as the human 73% of the time; the interrogators found the real human in only 27% of games against it[2].

The study also included, as a control, ELIZA, Joseph Weizenbaum’s program from 1966 that turns your sentences into questions. It was picked 23% of the time. In 1966 Weizenbaum had already noticed that “some subjects have been very hard to convince that ELIZA (with its present script) is not human”[3].

So a machine passes the test. Does it think? The answer depends on what you take thinking to be, and the most influential answer of the last eighty years is that thinking is computation: the mind is to the brain what a program is to the machine that runs it.

This is the computational theory of mind. It gave cognitive science its first research program and artificial intelligence its first name, and it has been attacked from the start on one question that language models have now made practical: can a system that manipulates symbols by their shapes ever mean anything by them?

Logic in the nervous system

The idea is older than computers. In 1943 the neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch and the logician Walter Pitts published “A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity”[4].

They simplified the neuron to a unit that adds its weighted inputs and fires if the sum reaches a threshold, and showed that networks of such units can compute any proposition of logic.

Three units suffice for AND, OR and NOT, and from those any Boolean function can be built. The neuron in this model is wrong in almost every biological detail, and the authors knew it.

The point was elsewhere: if neurons compute logical functions, then a brain is a kind of logic machine, and a thought might be a computation running on it.

Seven years earlier Turing had described a universal machine that can carry out any computation that can be written down as rules[5]. Put the two papers together and you get the founding bet of cognitive science: the brain implements a computer, and the mind is what it computes.

Symbols and search

The bet was stated most sharply by Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, whose Logic Theorist proved theorems from Principia Mathematica in 1956. Twenty years later, in their Turing Award lecture, they gave it the form of an empirical hypothesis[6]:

A physical symbol system has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action.

A physical symbol system is a machine that holds physical patterns, symbols, combines them into expressions, and runs processes that create, copy, modify and destroy those expressions. “Necessary” means that anything intelligent is such a system, people included.

“Sufficient” means that a large enough system of this kind, suitably organized, would be intelligent. Both halves are strong claims, and Newell and Simon offered them the way a physicist offers a law: to be tested against what intelligent systems actually do.

What does symbol processing look like in practice? Take a puzzle from Propositiones ad acuendos juvenes, “problems to sharpen the young”, a collection almost certainly by Alcuin of York from around 800 (MacTutor).

A man must take a wolf, a goat and a bundle of cabbages across a river in a boat that carries only two: him and one passenger. Left alone, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage.

For a symbol system the puzzle is a set of expressions, one per arrangement on the banks, and a rule that turns one arrangement into another. Solving it is searching:

The search finds what people find by trial and error: there are only ten safe arrangements, and two shortest solutions that differ in whether the wolf or the cabbage goes over first.

Newell and Simon’s claim is that this is not an analogy for what you did when you solved the puzzle as a child. It is a description of it, written at a different level of detail.

A language of thought

The philosopher Jerry Fodor turned the hypothesis into a theory of the mind as psychology knows it[7]. We explain behaviour by beliefs and desires: she took the umbrella because she believed it would rain and wanted to stay dry.

Fodor argued that this kind of explanation works because it is literally true. Beliefs and desires are real states of the brain, and they have the structure of sentences in an inner language, a language of thought, sometimes called Mentalese.

The hard part is how the content of a belief, what it is about, can cause anything. Fodor’s answer came from logic and computers.

A proof checker does not understand the formulas it checks; it looks at their shapes. Yet logicians have designed the rules so that whenever the premises are true, the conclusion the rules produce is true too.

Syntax, done right, keeps track of semantics. If the mind is such a system, then thoughts cause other thoughts by their shapes, and the causation respects what they mean.

Here is the idea in the smallest form, in an example from José Luis Bermúdez’s textbook Cognitive Science[8]. Let \(Ga\) say that Georgina is tall and \(Fa\) that she has red hair.

One rule joins two sentences with \(\wedge\); another replaces a name by a variable bound by “there exists”. Neither rule looks at what \(G\), \(F\) or \(a\) mean:

The check on the right is the whole point. Over every way the world could be, as far as these sentences can tell, the rules never lead from truths to a falsehood.

A rule that is not sound, such as concluding \(Gb\) from “someone is tall and red-haired”, fails in some world, and a well-built system simply does not have it.

Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn later turned this into an argument against the alternative that was then on the rise, neural networks[9].

Thought is systematic: “you don’t find people who can understand the sentence ‘John loves the girl’ but not the sentence ‘the girl loves John’”, and the same holds for thinking those thoughts. It is productive: from finite means we can think indefinitely many new thoughts. A language with combinatorial syntax explains both for free.

A network that learns associations, they argued, either implements such a language, and is then just its hardware (“models of the implementation of a Classical architecture”), or fails to be systematic. Their verdict was blunt: “the mind cannot be, in its general structure, a Connectionist network.”

The same question at three levels

Part of the confusion in this debate is that “the mind is a computer” can mean three different things. The vision scientist David Marr separated them[10].

At the level of computational theory you say what is computed and why: a cash register computes addition, because combining prices must not depend on their order or grouping.

At the level of representation and algorithm you say how: decimal digits and carrying, or binary and shifts. At the level of implementation you say what physically does it: gears, transistors, neurons.

The computational theory of mind is a claim about the first two levels. It is perfectly compatible with neurons being nothing like transistors. It is also why “but the brain is not a von Neumann computer” is not an objection: nobody serious claimed that it was.

The Chinese Room

The best-known objection grants the theory everything at the level of behaviour and denies it at the level of mind. In 1980 John Searle asked you to imagine yourself locked in a room with boxes of Chinese characters and a rule book in English[11]. Questions in Chinese come in through a slot.

You look up their shapes in the book, which tells you which shapes to send back, and you send them. The answers are good enough to fool native speakers. You do not understand a word of Chinese.

The room runs a program for understanding Chinese, Searle says, and nothing in it understands Chinese. So running a program is not sufficient for understanding.

He called the claim he was attacking strong AI: that an appropriately programmed computer literally has a mind. Weak AI, the use of computers to model and test theories of the mind, he had no quarrel with.

Searle listed the replies he had already heard and answered each one in the same paper:

  • The systems reply: you do not understand Chinese, but the whole system, you plus the book plus the paper, does. Searle: then memorize the book and do the lookups in your head. Now you are the whole system, and you still understand nothing.
  • The robot reply: put the program in a robot with cameras and arms, so its symbols connect to things. Searle: the man in the room now also receives symbols from cameras and sends symbols to motors. Still shapes.
  • The brain simulator reply: make the program simulate the firing of a Chinese speaker’s neurons. Searle: simulate it with water pipes and valves, operated by the man. The pipes do not understand Chinese either.

The argument is still argued about. One line of reply, from Paul and Patricia Churchland, is that intuitions about rooms are a poor guide to large systems: a person waving a magnet in a dark room produces electromagnetic waves too slow to see, and would conclude, wrongly, that light is not electromagnetism[12].

Searle had also anticipated neural networks: replace the room with a “Chinese gym”, a hall full of English speakers each doing what a unit does, and still nobody understands Chinese[13].

What he established beyond doubt is narrower than his conclusion, and still important: behaviour alone does not settle the question. In 1980 he had already granted that “there could be two ‘systems,’ both of which pass the Turing test, but only one of which understands”.

Where do symbols get their meaning?

Stevan Harnad sharpened Searle’s point into a problem that any theory has to solve, not just computational ones[14]. Imagine trying to learn Chinese from a Chinese-Chinese dictionary.

Every word is defined by other words, which are defined by other words, and you go round forever without touching anything. This is the symbol grounding problem: how do the symbols of a system come to be about things in the world, rather than only about each other?

Harnad’s own answer was that some symbols must be grounded in perception, in the categories that sensory systems learn to pick out.

Language models are the dictionary-go-round built at scale. They learn from text alone, and on Harnad’s view they should have no grounded meanings at all.

Emily Bender and Alexander Koller made the argument with an octopus that taps a telegraph cable between two islands and learns to imitate one of the speakers perfectly, until someone asks it for help against a bear[15]. Form, they argue, is not enough to learn meaning.

It turns out that form carries more than this suggests. Here is a small test you can run. Take fifty colour names, and for each the colour people mean by it, from an online survey in which over five million colours were named in 222,500 sessions[16].

Place the colours in CIELAB, a space built so that equal distances look equally different. Then take Qwen2.5-1.5B, a model that has never seen a colour, give it each name in a sentence, and compare the distances between its internal states:

The geometry is far from perfect, but it is there. Blues sit with blues, reds with reds and pinks, teal between green and blue.

The rank correlation between the two sets of distances is 0.38, and none of 2,000 shuffles of the words comes close. It is not an accident of one layer either:

The embedding layer knows little; from the sixth layer on, the model’s states keep a stable fraction of the colour space.

Abdou et al. (2021) found a modest but significant alignment of the same kind in several language models, and GPT-4’s judgments of how similar two colours are, given only their names, agree with people’s at r = 0.79[17].

Text is not as cut off from the world as the dictionary image suggests, because people wrote it about the world: about skies that were deep blue, and teal that sits between green and blue. Congenitally blind people show the same from the other side.

Asked how similar colour words are, they produce a map that resembles the colour space of sighted people[18], and they share sighted people’s understanding of what colours are for, learned from “living among people who talk about color”[19].

None of this answers Searle. A geometry of colour words is not the experience of red, and a system can have the first without the second. What it does change is the shape of the argument.

The question is no longer whether meaning can come from symbols alone, yes or no, but how much of it does, and which part can only come from somewhere else.

Networks, systematicity and language models

Fodor and Pylyshyn’s challenge to neural networks became testable. In 2018 Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni built SCAN, a set of commands such as “jump twice and walk left”, and trained sequence-to-sequence networks on it[20].

On a random split of the data the best network got 99.8% of new commands right. When “jump” appeared in training only on its own and had to be combined with the rest of the grammar at test time, the best network got 1.2%.

People do this effortlessly. Five years later the same authors trained a standard transformer on a stream of small composition tasks, each with its own made-up grammar, and on a new task it matched the algebraic answer as often as people did, or more[21].

They wrote that they had addressed “Fodor and Pylyshyn’s challenge”, and in the same paper listed what was left: much longer outputs and new sentence structures still defeated the model. Systematicity was not built in; it was learned from practice at being systematic.

Something similar shows up inside sequence models. A transformer trained only on lists of moves in the board game Othello, never shown a board, develops an internal representation of the board that can be read out and edited: change it, and the model’s next moves change as if the board were different[22].

Read as “my stones and the opponent’s” rather than “black and white”, the board can be recovered by a simple linear probe with 99.6% accuracy[23]. Othello is a toy world, fully determined by the moves, so this shows structure rather than reference to anything outside the text.

But it does show that such a network is not only associating surface forms. It builds structured states and computes with them, which is closer to what Fodor asked for than either side expected.

What the metaphor leaves out

The computational theory never lacked critics who thought it was looking in the wrong place. Hubert Dreyfus argued from the 1970s that human expertise rests on embodied know-how, not explicit rules[24].

The enactive tradition of Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson and Eleanor Rosch put the body and its activity at the centre[25]. More recent predictive processing theories describe the brain as a hierarchy that predicts its own sensory input and learns from the errors[26, 27].

Notice, though, that most of these are still computational at Marr’s first two levels. They disagree about what is computed and in what format, not about whether the mind computes.

The numbers also remind you how different the hardware is. A human brain has about 86 billion neurons[28], weighs about 2% of the body and uses about 20% of its oxygen[29].

That comes to roughly 20 watts, “a paltry sum given that the computer on which this article is being typed requires 80 W”, as the physicist Vijay Balasubramanian put it[30].

Which brings back the test. The interrogators who picked GPT-4.5 over a person were not wrong about anything they could check: the replies were what a person would write.

Turing proposed the game because he found “Can machines think?” “too meaningless to deserve discussion”, and behaviour was all anyone could go on. Seventy-five years later that is no longer true.

We can open the model, read off the board it keeps for Othello or the geometry it keeps for colour, and ask how much of a mind is in there, piece by piece. Searle’s room had no windows. This one does.

References

  1. Turing, A. M. (1950). Computing machinery and intelligence. Mind, 59(236), 433–460. ↩
  2. Jones, C. R., & Bergen, B. K. (2025). Large language models pass the Turing test. arXiv:2503.23674. ↩
  3. Weizenbaum, J. (1966). ELIZA: a computer program for the study of natural language communication between man and machine. Communications of the ACM, 9(1), 36–45. ↩
  4. McCulloch, W. S., & Pitts, W. (1943). A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity. Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics, 5, 115–133. ↩
  5. Turing, A. M. (1936). On computable numbers, with an application to the Entscheidungsproblem. Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, s2-42(1), 230–265. ↩
  6. Newell, A., & Simon, H. A. (1976). Computer science as empirical inquiry: symbols and search. Communications of the ACM, 19(3), 113–126. ↩
  7. Fodor, J. A. (1975). The Language of Thought. Crowell; Harvard University Press. ↩

  9. Fodor, J. A., & Pylyshyn, Z. W. (1988). Connectionism and cognitive architecture: a critical analysis. Cognition, 28(1–2), 3–71. ↩
  10. Marr, D. (1982). Vision. W. H. Freeman. ↩
