entry.summary: What happens in a brain that has a new idea, where recombination stops, and what the measurements of machine creativity show, from AlphaGo's move 37 to GPT-4 on the Alternate Uses Task

entry.title: The Algebra of LoRA
entry.content:
In section 7 of the paper that introduced LoRA there is a table its authors present with the words “To our surprise”. Edward Hu and colleagues at Microsoft had adapted GPT-3, all 175 billion parameters of it, by adding a trainable low-rank matrix to the query and value projections in each of its 96 layers, and they varied the rank.

At rank 1 the change to each \(12{,}288 \times 12{,}288\) matrix is the product of one column and one row: 24,576 numbers standing in for 151 million.

With it GPT-3 reached 73.4% on WikiSQL and 91.3% on MultiNLI; at rank 64, 73.5% and 91.4%. “A rank as small as one suffices for adapting both \(W_q\) and \(W_v\) on these datasets”, the caption concludes[1].

Two years later Damjan Kalajdzievski argued that the table proves less than it seems: the way LoRA scales its update, the paper showed, slows high ranks down so much that they could not have done better[2].

And in 2024 Dan Biderman and colleagues measured the changes that full fine-tuning makes to Llama 2 and found them to have “a rank that is 10-100× greater than typical LoRA configurations”[3].

So is a fine-tuning update low-rank or not? This post works through the linear algebra LoRA rests on: rank, the singular value decomposition, and the theorem that says how well a low-rank matrix can stand in for a full one.

Then through LoRA itself: why it starts the way it does, what its gradients see, and why a constant that looks like bookkeeping, the scale \(\alpha / r\), decides what a higher rank can do.

Every formula is checked, by a few lines of code or on a real model: bert-base fine-tuned on SST-2 48 times, with ranks from 1 to 256, two scaling rules, two learning-rate ratios and one factor frozen at a time. (If the transformer itself needs a refresher, the course Transformers: from scratch to production builds one; the adapters post puts LoRA among its relatives.)

What a matrix does

A weight matrix \(W\) with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns is a machine for turning vectors into vectors: it takes \(x\) with \(n\) coordinates and returns \(Wx\) with \(m\). In bert-base, the query projection of every attention layer takes the 768 numbers that describe a token and returns 768 others.

Matrices that size are impossible to picture, but a \(2 \times 2\) matrix can be watched at work. Feed it every point of the unit circle and see where they land:

Whatever the matrix, the circle becomes an ellipse, possibly a flat one. That is a general fact, and the most useful one in this post.

Every matrix, of any shape, does three things in a row: it turns the input, stretches it along perpendicular axes, and turns the result. This is the singular value decomposition (SVD):

\[W = U \Sigma V^\top = \sum_{i=1}^{\min(m,n)} \sigma_i \, u_i v_i^\top .\]

The columns \(v_i\) of \(V\) are perpendicular unit vectors in the input space (the grey arrows), and the columns \(u_i\) of \(U\) are perpendicular unit vectors in the output space. The singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0\) are the stretch factors: \(W v_i = \sigma_i u_i\), the rose arrows. In the left panel the input axes are stretched by 1.67 and 0.75.

The rank of \(W\) is the number of singular values that are not zero: the number of independent directions the matrix can write into. In the right panel \(\sigma_2 = 0\), and the circle collapses into a segment. Whatever the input, the output lies on one line, and pairs of points that differ only along \(v_2\) land on the same spot.

The rank is also the dimension of the space spanned by the columns of \(W\), and, less obviously, of the space spanned by its rows. The SVD shows why the two agree: the columns are combinations of \(u_1, \dots, u_r\) and the rows are combinations of \(v_1, \dots, v_r\), the same number \(r\) of vectors in both cases.

The middle panel matters most for what follows. Its rank is 2, but \(\sigma_2 = 0.03\): it is a rank-one map plus a correction too small to see.

Rank is a cliff, singular values are a slope. Matrices that come out of training are almost never exactly low-rank, but they are often close to it, and the singular values say how close.

Rank one: read one direction, write one direction

The simplest nonzero matrix is the product of a column and a row, \(u v^\top\). Applied to \(x\) it gives

\[u v^\top x = u \, (v^\top x) .\]

It measures \(x\) along one direction, \(v\) (the dot product \(v^\top x\) is a single number), and writes that number along another direction, \(u\). Everything in \(x\) perpendicular to \(v\) is ignored; nothing comes out that does not point along \(u\).

A matrix of rank \(r\) is a sum of \(r\) such read–write pairs. The SVD writes every matrix as such a sum, with the pairs perpendicular to each other and sorted by strength.

A product \(BA\), with \(B\) of shape \(m \times r\) and \(A\) of shape \(r \times n\), is the same thing in different clothes: \(BAx = B(Ax)\), so \(A\) reads \(r\) numbers out of \(x\) and \(B\) writes each of them along one of its \(r\) columns. Hence the inequality that LoRA rests on:

\[\operatorname{rank}(BA) \le \min\big(\operatorname{rank}(B), \operatorname{rank}(A)\big) \le r .\]

Every column of \(BA\) is a combination of the columns of \(B\), so there cannot be more independent ones than \(B\) has; every row of \(BA\) is a combination of the rows of \(A\), the same argument. Storing \(B\) and \(A\) takes \(r(m + n)\) numbers instead of \(mn\).

To see what a sum of rank-one layers looks like, take a matrix that is easy to look at: a grayscale photograph, 512 by 512 numbers between 0 and 1. Here it is rebuilt from the first \(k\) terms of its SVD:

Rank 1 is a plaid: one pattern of columns times one pattern of rows, which is all a single read–write pair can draw. It still holds 79% of the photo’s “energy”, \(\sum_i \sigma_i^2\), mostly the average brightness. Each further term adds one more pair.

By rank 16 there is a face, and at rank 64, stored in a quarter of the numbers, the error is 7%.

The best you can do with r directions

Is cutting the SVD after \(k\) terms the best possible rank-\(k\) approximation, or just a convenient one? It is the best.

The theorem carries the names of Carl Eckart and Gale Young, who proved it for matrices in 1936, in the first volume of Psychometrika, a journal of psychological measurement: they needed it to approximate tables of test scores by a few underlying factors[4].

As G. W. Stewart points out in a history of the SVD, they had rediscovered a result Erhard Schmidt published in 1907 for integral equations[5].

For a matrix \(M\) with singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots\) and its truncation \(M_k = \sum_{i \le k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top\),

\[\min_{\operatorname{rank}(X) \le k} \lVert M - X \rVert_F = \lVert M - M_k \rVert_F = \sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \sigma_{k+2}^2 + \dots + \sigma_{\min(m,n)}^2} ,\]

where \(\lVert \cdot \rVert_F\), the Frobenius norm, is the square root of the sum of the squares of all entries. Leon Mirsky extended the theorem in 1960 to every norm that does not change when the matrix is rotated[6].

In the spectral norm, the largest stretch a matrix applies to any unit vector, the smallest error is simply \(\sigma_{k+1}\).

Why squares under a square root? Because the rank-one layers are perpendicular to each other, as matrices. The inner product of two matrices, entry by entry, is \(\langle u_i v_i^\top, u_j v_j^\top \rangle = (u_i^\top u_j)(v_i^\top v_j)\), which is 0 for \(i \ne j\) and 1 for \(i = j\).

So Pythagoras applies: \(\lVert M \rVert_F^2 = \sum_i \sigma_i^2\), and dropping some layers leaves an error whose square is the sum of the squares of what was dropped.

The squares matter. The plain sum \(\sigma_{k+1} + \sigma_{k+2} + \dots\) is the error in another norm, the nuclear norm, and as a Frobenius error it is far too big: for the photograph at \(k = 16\) it gives 509, almost twice the size of the whole photograph, \(\lVert M \rVert_F = 272\), while the true error is 45.

The dots are errors measured by subtracting \(M_k\) from the photograph; the line is computed from the singular values alone, without looking at the approximation. They coincide, as the theorem says. The squares show what is lost by choosing the directions badly: keep 64 random directions instead of the best 64, and the error is 93%, not 7%.

This is the whole linear-algebra case for LoRA. If the change a task needs, \(\Delta W\), has singular values that fall quickly, a matrix of rank \(r\) can hold most of it, and the theorem says exactly how much is missed.

Whether real updates have quickly falling singular values is not a question linear algebra can answer. It is a question about training.

LoRA’s bet

The bet has a history. In 2018 Chunyuan Li and colleagues trained networks while letting the optimizer move only inside a random low-dimensional slice of the parameter space.

They called the smallest dimension that still reached 90% of the full solution the problem’s intrinsic dimension, and found it far smaller than the number of parameters: a small fully connected network for MNIST with 199,210 weights needed 750[7].

In 2020 Armen Aghajanyan, Luke Zettlemoyer and Sonal Gupta did the same with fine-tuning. RoBERTa-Large, with 355 million parameters, reached 90% of its full fine-tuning result on the paraphrase task MRPC by training about 200 numbers in such a slice[8].

Edward Hu and colleagues turned this into a parameterization[1]. Their hypothesis, in their words: “the change in weights during model adaptation also has a low ‘intrinsic rank’”. So instead of training \(W\), freeze it and train a low-rank change to it:

\[W = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}, \; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n} .\]

The saving depends on the shape. For a square \(n \times n\) matrix the full update has \(n^2\) numbers and the rank-\(r\) one \(2rn\), a ratio of \(n / 2r\):

matrix shape full update rank \(r\) LoRA’s numbers ratio
bert-base, query 768 × 768 589,824 8 12,288 48×
Llama 3 8B, q_proj 4,096 × 4,096 16,777,216 16 131,072 128×
GPT-3 175B, \(W_q\) 12,288 × 12,288 150,994,944 1 24,576 6,144×

For the whole model the ratio is larger still, because LoRA usually touches only some matrices and everything else is frozen. Hu et al. report that on GPT-3 175B it cut the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times, and the GPU memory needed for training by 3 times.

One layer, forward and back

Here is what happens inside one adapted layer, written with \(\gamma = \alpha / r\) for the scale:

\[h = W_0 x + \gamma \, B (A x) .\]

Training needs the gradients of the loss \(L\) with respect to \(B\) and \(A\). Write \(g = \partial L / \partial h\) for the gradient that arrives at the layer’s output, and \(z = Ax\) for the \(r\) numbers in the middle. Then \(h\) depends on \(B\) through \(\gamma B z\), and on \(A\) through \(z\), and the chain rule gives

\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial B} = \gamma \, g z^\top = \gamma \, g x^\top A^\top , \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial A} = \gamma \, B^\top g \, x^\top .\]

Summed over a batch, \(\sum g x^\top\) is exactly \(G = \partial L / \partial W\), the gradient that full fine-tuning would use to update \(W\). So

\[\nabla_B L = \gamma \, G A^\top , \qquad \nabla_A L = \gamma \, B^\top G .\]

LoRA does not compute a different gradient. It computes the same \(G\) and lets each factor see it through the other: \(B\) sees \(G\) through the \(r\) directions \(A\) reads, \(A\) sees it through the \(r\) directions \(B\) writes.

Formulas like these are easy to get wrong by a transpose, so here they are checked against PyTorch’s autograd:

import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)
d_out, d_in, r, gamma = 6, 5, 2, 0.5
W0 = torch.randn(d_out, d_in)
A = torch.randn(r, d_in, requires_grad=True)
B = torch.randn(d_out, r, requires_grad=True)  # not zero here, so that both gradients are nonzero
x = torch.randn(d_in, 4)  # four inputs, as columns

h = W0 @ x + gamma * B @ (A @ x)
loss = h.square().sum() / 2  # any loss would do; for this one dL/dh = h
loss.backward()

G = h.detach() @ x.T  # dL/dW: the gradient full fine-tuning would get
print(torch.allclose(B.grad, gamma * G @ A.T), torch.allclose(A.grad, gamma * B.T @ G))

True True

Why one factor starts at zero

Hu et al. start \(A\) random and \(B\) at zero. The formulas explain both halves of that choice.

\(B = 0\) makes \(\Delta W = BA = 0\), so training starts exactly from the pretrained model: no noise is added to a network that already works.

Why not set \(A = 0\) as well? Because then both gradients vanish, \(\nabla_B L = \gamma G A^\top = 0\) and \(\nabla_A L = \gamma B^\top G = 0\), and the factors never move: zero is a stationary point of the product.

With one factor random, the other one gets a gradient. At the first step that is \(B\): since \(B = 0\), \(\nabla_A L = 0\), so \(A\) stays where it was and only \(B\) moves.

The reverse, \(B\) random and \(A\) at zero, would also start at \(\Delta W = 0\) and also train; it is just not what the paper or the libraries do. The paper draws \(A\) from a Gaussian; Microsoft’s loralib and Hugging Face’s peft use a Kaiming-uniform distribution.

The first step, and why the scale matters

Follow the first steps of training with plain gradient descent at learning rate \(\eta\). On step one only \(B\) moves, to \(B_1 = -\eta \gamma \, G A_0^\top\), and the update becomes

\[\Delta W_1 = \gamma B_1 A_0 = -\eta \gamma^2 \, G A_0^\top A_0 .\]

Full fine-tuning would have taken the step \(-\eta G\). LoRA takes the same gradient and multiplies it, on the right, by \(A_0^\top A_0\): a square \(n \times n\) matrix of rank \(r\).

What does that matrix look like? Its entry \((j, k)\) is \(\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_{ij} a_{ik}\), a sum of \(r\) products of entries of \(A_0\).

If the entries are independent with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\), the diagonal entries are sums of \(r\) squares, \(r\sigma^2\) on average, and the off-diagonal ones are sums of products of independent numbers, 0 on average. So

\[\mathbb{E}\big[A_0^\top A_0\big] = r \sigma^2 I , \qquad \mathbb{E}\big[\Delta W_1\big] = -\eta \, \gamma^2 r \sigma^2 \, G .\]

On average, the first LoRA step is the full fine-tuning step, shrunk or stretched by the factor \(\gamma^2 r \sigma^2\). One draw of \(A_0\) is not its average, though:

With \(r\) rows, \(A_0^\top A_0\) keeps the components of the gradient along \(r\) random directions and drops the rest; its fluctuations around the identity shrink like \(1/\sqrt{r}\). In a 768-dimensional layer with \(r = 8\), the first step sees the full gradient through eight random windows.

Later steps are not so simple, because \(B\) is no longer zero and \(A\) starts to move too. To first order in \(\eta\), a general step changes the update by

\[\Delta W_{t+1} - \Delta W_t \approx -\eta \gamma^2 \left( G A^\top A + B B^\top G \right) ,\]

the full gradient, filtered on the right through the directions \(A\) reads and on the left through the directions \(B\) writes.

The scale

Now look at the size of that first step: it is proportional to \(\gamma^2 r\). With the paper’s \(\gamma = \alpha / r\) it is \(\alpha^2 / r\), so doubling the rank halves the effective learning rate, and a rank-256 adapter starts 256 times slower than a rank-1 one.

This is the argument of Damjan Kalajdzievski’s rsLoRA[2]. The paper proves, for gradient descent and in the limit of large \(r\), that the only scale under which an adapter’s outputs and gradients neither blow up nor die out as the rank grows is \(\gamma = \alpha / \sqrt{r}\), which keeps \(\gamma^2 r = \alpha^2\) for every rank.

And it draws the conclusion that brings us back to the start. The \(\alpha / r\) rule “slows the learning such that LoRA fine-tuning using larger ranks performs no different than that with very small ranks”, and this “may have led the authors of (Hu et al., 2022) to inaccurately conclude that very low ranks (e.g. 4,8,16) ‘suffice’”.

Almost nobody trains LoRA with plain gradient descent, though. The usual optimizer is Adam, which divides every coordinate’s gradient by a running estimate of its size, so that each parameter moves by about \(\eta\) per step whatever the scale of its gradient. That changes the arithmetic.

Now every entry of \(B\) moves by about \(\eta\), and every entry of \(\Delta W = \gamma B A\) is a sum of \(r\) such moves multiplied by entries of \(A\), with signs that mostly do not line up.

A sum of \(r\) terms of random sign grows like \(\sqrt{r}\). So under Adam the size of the update grows like \(\gamma \sqrt{r}\) instead of \(\gamma^2 r\), and the conclusion is the same: \(\alpha / r\) makes it shrink like \(1/\sqrt{r}\), \(\alpha / \sqrt{r}\) keeps it constant.

It also explains a remark of Hu et al.: “When optimizing with Adam, tuning α is roughly the same as tuning the learning rate if we scale the initialization appropriately.” Under Adam, \(\gamma\) multiplies the size of every step, just as \(\eta\) does.

Measuring it

All of this can be checked on a real model. I fine-tuned bert-base-uncased on SST-2, sentences from film reviews labelled positive or negative[9], with LoRA on the query and value projections of all 12 layers.

The setting is that of the adapters post: 10,000 training sentences, three epochs, AdamW at a learning rate of \(5 \times 10^{-4}\), batches of 32, three seeds per configuration, accuracy on the 872 validation sentences. For reference, full fine-tuning of all 110 million parameters reaches 91.4%.

The runs differ only in the algebra:

  • the rank, from 1 to 256;
  • the scale, \(\alpha / r\) with \(\alpha = 16\) as in the paper, or \(\alpha' / \sqrt{r}\) with \(\alpha'\) chosen so that the two agree at \(r = 8\);
  • which factor learns, and how fast.

The 48 runs took 40 minutes of training on a Kaggle T4 (experiment.py).

Rank under the two scales

First, the size of the update, \(\lVert \Delta W \rVert_F\) averaged over the 24 adapted matrices, as training goes:

At step 10 the prediction holds almost to the digit. Under \(\alpha / r\) the update of rank 1 has size 0.045 and that of rank 256 has 0.003, fifteen times smaller; the \(\gamma \sqrt{r}\) rule predicts \(\sqrt{256} = 16\). Under \(\alpha' / \sqrt{r}\) all six ranks start between 0.016 and 0.018.

Later the two pictures turn upside down. Under \(\alpha / r\) the lowest rank stays ahead all the way; under \(\alpha' / \sqrt{r}\) the highest ranks pull ahead, because they have more directions to grow in. What does that do to learning?

On the training set the two rules tell opposite stories. Under \(\alpha / r\) the loss at the end is the same for every rank from 4 to 256, 0.19: more rank buys nothing, the flat shape of Hu et al.’s table.

Under \(\alpha' / \sqrt{r}\) the loss keeps falling with rank, from 0.23 at \(r = 1\) to 0.12 at \(r = 256\): the extra directions are used.

On held-out sentences the effect is smaller, because SST-2 is easy for BERT and a few directions are enough to tell praise from complaint. Under \(\alpha / r\) accuracy stays between 90.3% and 90.9% at every rank, about half a point under full fine-tuning. Under \(\alpha' / \sqrt{r}\) it climbs to 91.4% at ranks 64 and 256, level with full fine-tuning.

The gap is small: three seeds per point, and a single validation sentence is worth 0.11%. But compared seed by seed at ranks 64 and 256, the rank-stabilized run is ahead five times out of six, and the sixth is a tie.

So both papers are right about different things. On this task a low rank does suffice, as Hu et al. found; and the \(\alpha / r\) rule does hide what higher ranks could add, as Kalajdzievski argued.

In Hugging Face’s peft the corrected scale is one flag. The lesson for practice: if you raise the rank, either switch the scale or raise \(\alpha\) with it.

from peft import LoraConfig

config = LoraConfig(r=64, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["query", "value"],
                    use_rslora=True)  # scale lora_alpha / sqrt(r) instead of lora_alpha / r

Two factors, two learning rates

The initialization treats the factors differently, and two later papers argue that training should too.

Jiacheng Zhu and colleagues found that “A extracts features from the input, while B uses these features to create the desired output”, and that “a random untrained A should perform nearly as well as a fine-tuned one”[10].

Soufiane Hayou, Nikhil Ghosh and Bin Yu showed that in very wide networks one learning rate cannot be right for both factors, and proposed LoRA+: give \(B\) a learning rate \(\lambda\) times that of \(A\)[11].

The best \(\lambda\) depends on the model, the task and the initialization. With LoRA’s standard start they found it around 4 to 8, and up to 16 with the factors’ roles swapped.

On BERT and SST-2 neither shortcut pays.

\(A\) does not stay near its random start: by the end of training it has moved by 70% of its initial size.

Freezing it costs 2.2 points (88.7% against 90.9%), with half as many trained numbers; freezing \(B\) and training \(A\) costs 2.6. The asymmetry Zhu et al. describe is there, but it is small next to the price of freezing either factor.

LoRA+ with \(\lambda = 4\) reaches 91.0% against 90.9%, and after the first epoch 90.1% against 89.9%; with \(\lambda = 16\) it is a little worse. Hayou et al. write that the benefits are larger “for ‘hard’ tasks such as MNLI … (compared to SST2 for instance)”, and this is SST-2.

What the update looks like

Hu et al. ended their paper with questions about \(\Delta W\) itself: does a higher rank find new directions or the same ones, and how does \(\Delta W\) relate to \(W\)? Both can be asked of BERT.

For the first, they compared the subspaces spanned by \(A\) in a rank-8 and a rank-64 run, with a measure that is 1 when one subspace contains the other and 0 when they are perpendicular:

\[\varphi(i, j) = \frac{\lVert U_i^\top U_j' \rVert_F^2}{\min(i, j)} ,\]

where \(U_i\) holds the top \(i\) right singular vectors of one \(A\) and \(U_j'\) the top \(j\) of the other. In plain words, it is the average squared cosine between the two sets of directions.

The result repeats theirs. The single strongest direction of the rank-8 run lies largely inside the rank-64 run: the median \(\varphi(1, 1)\) over the 24 matrices is 0.54, where Hu et al. report “> 0.5” for GPT-3.

The agreement fades quickly after it. By \(i = 8\) it is 0.13, more than ten times the 0.01 that random directions would give but far from 1. Two rank-64 runs with different seeds share less, 0.33 for the top direction.

Hu et al. read the pattern as a sign that the top directions carry the adaptation, while the others “potentially contain mostly random noises accumulated during training”.

For the second question, project \(W\) onto the update’s top \(r\) directions, \(\lVert U^\top W V \rVert_F\) with \(U, V\) the update’s singular vectors, and compare it with \(\lVert \Delta W \rVert_F\). Hu et al. call the ratio the amplification factor: a large one means the update makes a big change in directions where \(W\) itself is weak.

The shape again matches theirs, at a smaller scale. The rank-8 update’s directions are barely more aligned with \(W\) than random ones (1.2 times, while \(W\)’s own top 8 directions carry 28 times more), so the update does not reinforce what \(W\) already does strongly.

In those directions it is about five times larger than \(W\): the median factor is 4.9, where Hu et al. measured 21.5 for rank 4 on GPT-3.

At rank 64 the factor drops below 1, as in their paper it dropped to about 2. Full fine-tuning behaves differently: its top 8 directions are more aligned with \(W\) (2.3 times random), and the update in them is small, a third of \(W\) there.

Finally, the singular values, where the rank inequality from the beginning becomes visible:

The rank-8 update has eight singular values and then a cliff to \(10^{-9}\), rounding error: \(\operatorname{rank}(BA) \le 8\), measured.

The update full fine-tuning makes has no cliff. Its top 8 directions hold 37% of its energy \(\sum_i \sigma_i^2\), its top 64 hold 70%, and reaching 90% takes 193 directions, the same numbers as in the adapters post’s separate run.

It is also small: its norm is a sixth of LoRA’s (0.31 against 1.9 on average), since LoRA trains with a 25 times larger learning rate and packs the change into fewer directions.

And the two updates mostly point to different places: only 16% of full fine-tuning’s update (by norm) lies in the subspaces the rank-8 LoRA chose, against 1% for random subspaces of that size.

Biderman et al. draw the same line between the two questions: “the rank needed to reconstruct the weight matrix is higher than the rank needed for a downstream task.”

After training: merge, swap, add

When training ends, \(\gamma BA\) is just a matrix of the same shape as \(W_0\). Adding it in, \(W = W_0 + \gamma BA\), gives an ordinary model with no extra layers and no extra cost at inference: “no inference latency … by construction”, in the paper’s words.

Merging is exact. In the adapters post the merged BERT gave the same outputs as the unmerged one to within \(2.1 \times 10^{-6}\), rounding error in 32-bit arithmetic.

Unmerged, the factors are a small file. On GPT-3, with \(r = 4\) on \(W_q\) and \(W_v\), a task costs 35 MB instead of a 350 GB copy of the model, so one base model and a hundred tasks take 354 GB instead of 35 TB.

Since merging and unmerging are exact, a server can keep one base model and swap updates in and out. The catch, which Hu et al. state themselves: once \(BA\) is folded into \(W\), “it is not straightforward to batch inputs to different tasks with different A and B in a single forward pass”.

Keep the factors separate instead, and every request in a batch can use its own: \(h = W_0 x + \gamma B_k A_k x\) costs two thin products per request. S-LoRA turned that into a serving system that keeps thousands of adapters in memory and batches requests that use different ones[12].

Updates can also be added. Two of them, \(\gamma B_1 A_1 + \gamma B_2 A_2\), are one LoRA of rank \(r_1 + r_2\):

\[B_1 A_1 + B_2 A_2 = \begin{bmatrix} B_1 & B_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} A_1 \\ A_2 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

so “stacking” adapters adds nothing a larger rank could not do. The algebra of the sum is exact; whether the sum works is a different question.

  • Gabriel Ilharco and colleagues added whole fine-tuning updates (“task vectors”) for different image tasks. They found the updates “typically close to orthogonal”, and speculated that this is what lets them be added “with minimal interference”[13].
  • When updates do overlap, they fight. TIES-Merging traces the losses to redundant changes and to disagreements in sign[14].
  • LoraHub learns weights for combining LoRA modules from a few examples, and mixes the factors, \((\sum_i w_i B_i)(\sum_j w_j A_j)\)[15]. That is not the same as mixing the updates: the product expands into \(\sum_i w_i^2 B_i A_i\) plus cross terms \(w_i w_j B_i A_j\) that belong to neither adapter.

The family

Most of LoRA’s many descendants change one piece of the algebra above. A short map:

method what it changes the update
rsLoRA[2] the scale \(\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{r}} BA\)
LoRA+[11] the learning rates \(B\) learns \(\lambda\) times faster than \(A\)
AdaLoRA[16] the rank, per matrix, during training \(P \Lambda Q\), entries of \(\Lambda\) pruned by importance
DoRA[17] length and direction, separately \(m \, \frac{W_0 + BA}{\lVert W_0 + BA \rVert_c}\)
VeRA[18] which factors are trained \(\Lambda_b B \Lambda_d A\), with \(B, A\) random, frozen and shared
PiSSA[19] the initialization \(BA\) starts as the top-\(r\) SVD of \(W_0\)
QLoRA[20] the frozen part \(W_0\) stored in 4 bits

The first two were measured above. The others, in a few words each.

AdaLoRA writes the update in the shape of an SVD, \(P \Lambda Q\), with a penalty that keeps \(P\) and \(Q\) close to orthogonal. During training it zeroes the “singular values” in \(\Lambda\) whose removal would hurt the loss least, so that important matrices end up with a higher rank[16].

DoRA splits each column of the weight matrix into a length \(m\) and a direction (\(\lVert \cdot \rVert_c\) is the length of each column). It trains the lengths directly and the directions with LoRA[17].

VeRA goes further than “only B”: both factors are random, frozen and shared by all layers, and each layer trains two vectors that scale their rows and columns. A layer then costs \(d + r\) numbers instead of \(2dr\)[18].

PiSSA is Eckart–Young put to work. It starts \(B\) and \(A\) from the top \(r\) singular directions of \(W_0\) itself and freezes the remainder, the error matrix of the best rank-\(r\) approximation, so that training starts on the directions in which \(W_0\) is largest[19].

LoftQ uses the same theorem to choose \(B\) and \(A\) so that they compensate for the error of quantizing \(W_0\)[21].

QLoRA leaves the algebra alone and changes the storage: the frozen \(W_0\) is kept in 4 bits, the factors in 16, so a 65-billion-parameter model can be fine-tuned on one 48 GB GPU[20].

Summing up

LoRA rests on one inequality, \(\operatorname{rank}(BA) \le r\), and one theorem, Eckart and Young’s, which says what a matrix of rank \(r\) can and cannot hold.

The rest follows from writing the update as a product: gradients that see the full gradient through two narrow windows, a start that must set one factor to zero and not both, and a scale that quietly decides how fast each rank learns.

On BERT and SST-2 the measurements side with both camps. A rank between 1 and 8 gets within a point of full fine-tuning, as Hu et al. found on GPT-3. And the original \(\alpha / r\) makes higher ranks look useless when, scaled by \(\alpha / \sqrt{r}\), they keep improving.

The change full fine-tuning makes is not low-rank. The change a task needs is often close to it, and how close depends on the task: Hu et al. themselves warn that “we do not expect a small r to work for every task or dataset”.

References

  1. Hu et al., 2021. arxiv.org. ↩
  2. Kalajdzievski, 2023. arxiv.org. ↩
  3. Biderman et al., 2024. arxiv.org. ↩
  4. Eckart & Young, 1936. doi.org. ↩
  5. Stewart, 1993. doi.org. ↩
  6. Mirsky, 1960. doi.org. ↩
  7. Li et al., 2018. arxiv.org. ↩
  8. Aghajanyan et al., 2021. arxiv.org. ↩
  9. Socher et al., 2013. aclanthology.org. ↩
  10. Zhu et al., 2024. arxiv.org. ↩
  11. Hayou et al., 2024. arxiv.org. ↩
  12. Sheng et al., 2023. arxiv.org. ↩
  13. Ilharco et al., 2023. arxiv.org. ↩
  14. Yadav et al., 2023. arxiv.org. ↩
  15. Huang et al., 2023. arxiv.org. ↩

entry.summary: Why a fine-tuning update can be the product of two thin matrices: rank, the singular value decomposition and the Eckart–Young theorem, then LoRA's initialization, gradients and scale, derived by hand and checked on BERT

entry.title: LLMs for Those Who Missed Out

link.title: LLMs for Those Who Missed Out

entry.content:
In 2023 the lawyers of a man suing the airline Avianca filed a brief in a New York federal court. It cited earlier decisions that the other side could not find, and neither could the judge.

One of the lawyers, Steven Schwartz, had found them with ChatGPT, and had even checked: “Is Varghese a real case?” ChatGPT replied that the case “does indeed exist” and could be found “on Westlaw and LexisNexis”.

It did not exist. In June the court fined the lawyers and their firm $5,000, and the judge called the legal analysis in one of the invented opinions “gibberish”[1].

The judge was careful to add that “there is nothing inherently improper about using a reliable artificial intelligence tool for assistance”. The trouble was what the lawyers took the tool to be: a database of court decisions. It is not one.

This post is about what a large language model actually is. It follows a talk Andrej Karpathy recorded in November 2023 for people who had not been following the field, “Intro to Large Language Models” (video, slides).

The route is the same: what a model is made of, the three stages of training, what models can do, how they fail. Along the way I check the claims against their sources and measure some of them on small open models that run on a laptop.

Two files

Karpathy starts with a surprise: a language model you can download is two files. One holds the parameters. For Llama 2 70B, which Meta released in July 2023 with its weights open, that is 70 billion numbers, each stored in two bytes: 140 GB.

The other file is a program that reads those numbers and uses them to compute what text should come next. It is short.

Karpathy’s own llama2.c began in July 2023 as a single C file of 492 lines with no dependencies; the version current today has 973. (It also computes in 32 bits, and its README warns that models larger than 7B will not load productively.)

Everything the model knows is in the first file, and none of it is readable. There are no facts in there, only numbers that the program multiplies with other numbers.

Running the model needs no internet, only enough memory to hold the parameters, and that is the catch. 140 GB is more than any laptop has: the largest MacBook Pro tops out at 128 GB[2]. Karpathy’s demo in the talk was the 7B model, and Karpathy notes that 70B would run “about 10 times slower”.

What makes 70B fit is rounding. Store every parameter in 4 bits instead of 16, in the format of the open-source program llama.cpp, and the model shrinks to 39 GB (GGUF files). That fits in a 64 GB MacBook Pro, at a small cost in accuracy.

A note on words: Llama 2 is not open source in the usual sense. Its license forbids, for instance, using its outputs to improve other models, and the Open Source Initiative says it is “very plainly not an ‘Open Source’ license”[3]. “Open weights” is the accurate term.

Stage one: pretraining

The parameters are cheap to run and expensive to make. Karpathy’s slide gives round numbers for Llama 2 70B: about 10 TB of text, about 6,000 GPUs, about 12 days, about two million dollars.

These are Karpathy’s estimates. Meta’s paper gives the measured version: 2 trillion tokens of training text and 1,720,320 hours of A100 GPU time for the 70B model[4]. Six thousand GPUs for twelve days is 1.73 million GPU-hours, so the round numbers hold up.

And Karpathy called them “rookie numbers”. Llama 3, released last week, was trained on “over 15T tokens”, seven times as much, and its 70B model took 6.4 million hours on newer H100 GPUs[5]. The closed models are bigger still, by estimates only, since their makers do not publish them:

One question, asked again and again

What does all that computation teach the model? One skill: given a piece of text, assign a probability to every possible next token, a word or a piece of a word. Here is a small open model, TinyLlama, with 1.1 billion parameters trained on about a trillion tokens three times over[6]:

“Can” gets 48%, and it is only the first of three pieces: the model reads and writes “Canberra” as “Can”, “ber”, “ra”. “Sydney” gets 10%. That is the popular mistake, and it lives in the model as a probability, learned from all the text that gets the capital wrong.

To write, the program asks the same question again and again. It picks a token, appends it to the text, and asks for the next one:

Always taking the most likely token, the model finishes the sentence, starts a new line and writes the same sentence again, more sure of itself the second time. Repetition is a well-known failure of this “greedy” choice.

Chatbots instead draw each token at random, in proportion to its probability, which is also why the same question can get different answers, and why one answer in ten might say Sydney.

Prediction is compression

Karpathy describes pretraining as compressing the internet into the parameters, “kind of like a zip file”. The comparison is more literal than it sounds.

A model that gives probability \(p\) to the token that actually comes next can encode that token in \(-\log_2 p\) bits, with a method called arithmetic coding, and decode it back exactly.

The better the predictions, the shorter the code. Grégoire Delétang and colleagues at Google DeepMind took this seriously: Chinchilla, a 70-billion-parameter model, compresses a gigabyte of Wikipedia to 8.3% of its size, where gzip gets 32.3%[7].

I tried the same on a text none of these models could have seen: an earlier draft of this post, written this month.

gzip needs 3.65 bits per character. GPT-2, from 2019, needs 1.20; TinyLlama, 0.86, about a quarter of gzip. The Pythia models were all trained on the same data in the same order[8], so they differ only in size, and every step up in size gives a shorter code.

There is a catch the chart leaves out: to decode, you need the model, and TinyLlama’s parameters take 2.2 GB, three hundred thousand times more than the text.

As a practical compressor a language model is absurd; Delétang et al. count the parameters in and get rates in the thousands of percent. As a measure of how much a model has learned about text, the code length is exact.

Lossy

Arithmetic coding with a model is lossless. What is lossy is the model itself as a summary of its training data: 2 trillion tokens do not fit into 140 GB. Karpathy puts the ratio at roughly a hundred to one.

What the model keeps is closer to the gist of the data than to the data, and when asked for details it does not have, it produces text with the shape of the details:

TinyLlama knows the form of the answer, a name, and it knows that Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman go together. Large models make the same kind of error less often, but they make it, as the lawyers in New York found out.

There is a stranger failure. Karpathy’s example: GPT-4 knows that Tom Cruise’s mother is Mary Lee Pfeiffer, but asked who Mary Lee Pfeiffer’s son is, it says it does not know. Lukas Berglund and colleagues called this the reversal curse and measured it on celebrity parents: GPT-4 named the parent 79% of the time and the child 33%[9].

Why would a model know a fact one way round and not the other? It learned the fact from text in which Tom Cruise comes first and Mary Lee Pfeiffer second, and training on “A is B” makes B more likely after A, not A after B. Berglund et al. tested this directly.

They fine-tuned GPT-3 and Llama-1 on invented facts such as “Uriah Hawthorne is the composer of Abyssal Melodies”, and the models could not answer “Who composed Abyssal Melodies?”: the right name was no more likely than a random one.

Put the same fact into the prompt, though, and the models reverse it without trouble. What a model learned in training and what is in front of it in the text behave differently, and that difference comes back below, with tools.

Stage two: from a document completer to an assistant

A model fresh from pretraining continues documents. Asked a question, it keeps writing the page the question might have come from:

The base model repeats the question, answers it, and repeats the pair, the way a page of quiz questions would. The chat version answers, once. The difference comes from a second, much smaller round of training on conversations written by people, in which the model learns the format and tone of an assistant.

OpenAI’s InstructGPT, the predecessor of ChatGPT, was trained this way on about 13,000 prompts with answers written by “a team of 40 contractors”. Labellers preferred the answers of the 1.3-billion-parameter result to those of the original 175-billion-parameter GPT-3[10].

Meta stopped at 27,540 annotated examples for Llama 2, under a heading that says it all: “Quality Is All You Need”. Karpathy’s slide says “~100K conversations”; for Llama 3, Meta reports “over 10M human-annotated examples” across all of its fine-tuning.

The bottom row of the figure shows what the chat model actually receives. The question is wrapped in markers, <|user|> and <|assistant|>, and the model completes the document as before.

Fine-tuning did not change what the model does, only which documents it expects. Because this stage is cheap, Karpathy notes that companies can repeat it “every week”, while pretraining happens perhaps once a year.

Stage three: comparing instead of writing

It is easier to judge a haiku than to write one. The Llama 2 paper puts it this way: “while we may not all be accomplished artists, our ability to appreciate and critique art remains intact”. (TinyLlama’s haiku above is not 5-7-5, and anyone can see it.)

So the third stage collects judgments. People are shown two answers to the same prompt and pick the better one. Meta collected 1,418,091 such comparisons for Llama 2.

A separate reward model is trained to predict the choices, and the chat model is then trained, with reinforcement learning, to write answers the reward model scores highly.

The method is reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). OpenAI made it famous with InstructGPT, but it goes back to a 2017 paper by researchers from OpenAI and DeepMind together[11].

In 2023 a shortcut appeared, direct preference optimization (DPO), which learns from the same comparisons without a reward model[12]. TinyLlama’s chat version was trained with it, on comparisons ranked by GPT-4 instead of people (model card).

Who is ahead

How do you rank chatbots? The most trusted answer in 2024 is a tournament. On Chatbot Arena, run by the LMSYS group at Berkeley, a visitor asks a question, two anonymous models answer, and the visitor votes for the better one.

From the votes, more than 240,000 by January, the site fits a rating like a chess player’s Elo[13].

In November 2023 Karpathy’s slide showed the closed models, GPT-4 and Claude, well above every model with open weights.

In late March Claude 3 Opus became the first model to share the top spot with GPT-4. Then, last Thursday, Meta released Llama 3. This is the board on Monday:

Llama 3 70B, whose weights anyone can download, sits fifth: below the GPT-4 Turbo versions and Claude 3 Opus, above Claude 3 Sonnet and the original GPT-4 of March 2023.

Llama 2 70B, the open model of Karpathy’s talk, is at the bottom of this list. The gap between closed and open has not closed, but in a year it shrank from a wide margin to a few dozen rating points.

The choice between them is still the one Karpathy described. Closed models are rented through a website or an API.

Some can be fine-tuned through the API (OpenAI has offered this for GPT-3.5 since August 2023), and in November OpenAI added custom “GPTs”, ChatGPT with your own instructions and files, followed in January by a store for them. Open weights can be downloaded, run privately, and changed without asking anyone.

Tools and senses

A language model on its own is bad at arithmetic and knows nothing after its training data ends. Both problems have the same fix: let it call programs. The model writes a request in an agreed format, the program around it runs the tool, and the result is pasted back into the text for the model to read:

This is the lesson of the reversal curse put to work: what the model cannot recall from training, it can still use when the text in front of it contains it.

Researchers showed in early 2023 that a model can teach itself when to call a calculator or a search engine[14]. In March 2023 OpenAI opened ChatGPT to plugins, later replaced by GPTs; plugins were switched off this month.

The tools that remain built in are web search through Bing, a Python sandbox for analysis and charts, and DALL·E 3 for images.

Karpathy’s demo strings them together: it searches for a startup’s funding rounds, computes the missing valuations with a calculator, plots them with Python, extrapolates the trend, and draws a logo.

The senses arrived in the same year:

  • Images in. Since September 2023 ChatGPT can look at photos[15], and since March 2024 so can Claude 3[16].
  • Voice. ChatGPT talks, but through a pipeline: a speech recognizer, Whisper, writes down what you say, and a separate speech synthesizer reads the answer aloud.
  • Long inputs. Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro, in testing since February, reads up to a million tokens: “1 hour of video, 11 hours of audio” or a stack of books[17].
  • Video out. Not yet. OpenAI showed Sora in February, a model that generates minute-long videos, but has given it only to testers and a few artists[18].

Thinking slowly

Daniel Kahneman, who died last month, described the mind with two characters. “System 1 operates automatically and quickly, with little or no effort.” System 2 takes over for “effortful mental activities”, such as the book’s example 17 × 24: you know at once that it is a multiplication, but the answer, 408, takes work[19].

A language model, Karpathy says, has only a System 1. Every token costs the same fixed amount of computation, whether the question is “2 + 2” or a proof. The model cannot stop and think before it writes; it can only write.

But writing can stand in for thinking. Ask a model to reason step by step, and the intermediate steps become part of the text it reads before answering. Adding one sentence, “Let’s think step by step”, raised an OpenAI model’s score on simple arithmetic word problems from 17.7% to 78.7%[20].

The next step is to let the model try several lines of reasoning, judge them, and back up from dead ends, as a person does with a hard puzzle. Shunyu Yao and colleagues called this a tree of thoughts and tested it on the Game of 24:

Answering at once, GPT-4 solved 7% of the puzzles; reasoning step by step, 4%. Searching through a tree of partial solutions, judging each with the model itself, it solved 74%[21]. It costs far more computation per answer.

Karpathy’s wish is a model you can tell to take thirty minutes and come back with a better answer; no product offers that today.

Can a model teach itself?

In March 2016 DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the strongest Go players in the world, 4–1. It learned in two stages.

First it imitated people: a network trained on 30 million positions from online games learned to predict the expert’s move 57% of the time. Then it played against itself, and the self-taught version won more than 80% of its games against the imitator[22].

A year later DeepMind dropped the first stage. AlphaGo Zero started from random play, learned only from games against itself, and after three days beat the version that had beaten Lee Sedol 100 games to 0[23]:

Language models, Karpathy says, are still in AlphaGo’s first stage: they imitate people. The obstacle to the second is the “lack of a reward criterion in the general case”.

Go has an exact one, the game is won or lost. “Was this a good essay?” has none.

Where a check exists, the second stage has begun:

  • Geometry. AlphaGeometry trained on 100 million synthetic theorems with proofs it generated itself, and solved 25 of 30 olympiad geometry problems[24].
  • Mathematics by program. FunSearch paired a language model with a program that scores its proposals and found larger “cap sets”, a problem in combinatorics, than mathematicians had[25].
  • Models as judges. Anthropic’s Constitutional AI replaces human judgments of harmlessness with judgments by a model following written principles[26]. In January Meta reported a Llama 2 70B that improves by grading its own answers[27].

Attacks

The last part of Karpathy’s talk is about security, and it is the part most people skip. A model that follows instructions in text will follow instructions from anyone who can put text in front of it.

  • Jailbreaks. Safety training is a habit, not a lock. In April 2023 people got Discord’s chatbot to explain how to make napalm by asking it to play their late grandmother, who used to tell them about her work at a napalm factory[28]. The same request encoded in Base64 slips past refusals that were trained mostly on plain English[29].
  • Adversarial suffixes. A string of nonsense characters, found by optimizing against open models, makes closed ones comply too; in the paper’s tests it worked on GPT-3.5 86.6% of the time[30]. A slightly altered image of a panda does the same to a model that reads images[31].
  • Prompt injection. A web page, an email or a shared document can contain instructions aimed at the model that reads it. Such applications “blur the line between data and instructions”[32]; one researcher got Google’s Bard to leak a user’s data through a shared Google Doc[33].
  • Poisoned data. As few as 100 poisoned examples in fine-tuning data can make a model misbehave whenever a trigger phrase, “James Bond” in the paper’s example, appears[34]. In January Anthropic showed that such hidden behaviour can survive standard safety training[35].
  • Long contexts. And three weeks ago Anthropic described “many-shot jailbreaking”: fill a long context window with hundreds of fake dialogues in which an assistant complies, and the real one starts to comply as well[36].

Karpathy is careful to say that many of these specific attacks have been patched. The pattern has not: every new ability, from reading images to reading a million tokens, is also a new way in.

What comes next

Karpathy ends with a picture: the language model as the kernel of a new operating system. The context window is its working memory, the tools are its devices, and the model decides what to load and what to run. The talk’s list of what such a system will soon do reads, five months later, like this:

  • read and write text, browse the internet and use existing software: done, through tools;
  • see and generate images: done; generate video: shown, not released;
  • hear and speak: done, through a pipeline of separate models;
  • think for a long time before answering: not yet, beyond research such as Tree of Thoughts;
  • improve itself where success can be checked: in research, in geometry and mathematics;
  • be customized and sold in an app store: done, as GPTs;
  • talk to other models: in research frameworks.

The other half of the operating-system picture is the market. On one side are the closed systems, like Windows and macOS; on the other, open weights, like Linux, now a few dozen rating points behind.

Whichever wins, the lawyers’ lesson holds. What is on the other side of the chat window is not a database. It is a very good predictor of the next word, trained on most of what people have written.

entry.summary: What a large language model is, how it is made in three stages, and what it could and could not do in spring 2024: a tour after Andrej Karpathy's talk, with the claims checked against their sources and measured on small open models

entry.title: How to Write Good Python Code

link.title: How to Write Good Python Code

entry.content:
Python is a fantastic programming language!

It can be used for many things, like building websites, exploring data, and teaching machines to learn.

If you already know Python or are just beginning, writing code that is strong, easy to read, and easy to keep up with is important.

In this bogpost, we’ll look at the basic rules for writing great Python code and share some tips to help you make your programs even better.

📚 Use Meaningful Naming Conventions

One of the most important aspects of good Python code is meaningful naming conventions.

Choosing descriptive and concise names for variables, functions, and classes can help make your code more readable and understandable.

Using proper naming conventions can also help you avoid naming conflicts, reduce the risk of errors, and simplify maintenance.

For example, these are bad variable names:

x = 5
y = 10
z = x + y
w = z * 2

And these are better ones:

first_number = 5
second_number = 10
sum_of_numbers = first_number + second_number
double_sum = sum_of_numbers * 2

This includes using proper indentation, white space, line breaks, and following a code style guide like the PEP 8 style guide.

Clear, organized code makes it easier to understand and modify and reduces the risk of errors.

Here’s an example of lousy code organization:

def calc_sum(a, b, c, d):
    return a + b + c + d
def calc_diff(a, b, c, d):
    return a - b - c - d
def calc_product(a, b, c, d):
    return a * b * c * d
def calc_quotient(a, b, c, d):
    return a / b / c / d
def process_data(a, b, c, d):
    s = calc_sum(a, b, c, d)
    d = calc_diff(a, b, c, d)
    p = calc_product(a, b, c, d)
    q = calc_quotient(a, b, c, d)
    print("Sum: ", s)
    print("Difference: ", d)
    print("Product: ", p)
    print("Quotient: ", q)

And here’s an example of good code organization:

def calc_sum(a, b, c, d):
    return a + b + c + d

def calc_diff(a, b, c, d):
    return a - b - c - d

def calc_product(a, b, c, d):
    return a * b * c * d

def calc_quotient(a, b, c, d):
    return a / b / c / d

def process_data(a, b, c, d):
    s = calc_sum(a, b, c, d)
    d = calc_diff(a, b, c, d)
    p = calc_product(a, b, c, d)
    q = calc_quotient(a, b, c, d)
    
    results = {
        "Sum": s,
        "Difference": d,
        "Product": p,
        "Quotient": q
    }
    
    return results

💬 Write Comments

Adding comments to your code is a great way to explain what it does and provide context for other developers.

Comments should be used to explain complex code, provide additional information about the purpose of the code, and describe your thought process.

Writing comments can also help you better understand your code when you return to it later.

def calc_sum(a, b):
    # function to calculate sum
    c = a + b
    return c

# this function calculates sum of two numbers
def calc_difference(a, b):
    return a - b

The comments are not very descriptive or helpful in understanding the purpose of the functions.

The first comment is trivial and adds no additional information. The second comment repeats what the function name already tells us.

def calc_sum(a, b):
    """
    This function calculates the sum of two numbers `a` and `b`.
    The function takes in two keyword arguments, `a` and `b`, and returns their sum.
    """
    # calculate the sum of `a` and `b`
    c = a + b
    return c

def calc_difference(a, b):
    """
    This function calculates the difference between two numbers `a` and `b`.
    The function takes in two keyword arguments, `a` and `b`, and returns the difference of `a` and `b`.
    """
    # calculate the difference between `a` and `b`
    return a - b

The comments provide a clear and concise explanation of the purpose and behaviour of each function.

The use of docstrings makes it easy to understand what the functions do and what arguments they take in. This makes the code more readable and maintainable.

🧰 Use Modules and Packages

Modules and packages are a great way to organize your code into reusable blocks.

They allow you to group related code together and make it easier to manage, understand, and maintain.

The Python Standard Library is an good resource for finding pre-existing modules and packages. You can import it into your programs to save time and effort.

Consider a project to build a simple weather application that provides a given city’s current temperature and conditions. We can structure the project as follows:

weather_app/
    __init__.py
    weather.py
    utils/
        __init__.py
        api.py
        data_processing.py

weather.py is the main module that the user interacts with, which provides a single function to get the current weather information.

def get_current_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    """
    Gets the current weather information for the given city.

    Args:
        city (str): The city for which to get the weather information.

    Returns:
        dict: The weather information for the given city.
    """
    weather_data = utils.api.get_weather_data(city)
    processed_data = utils.data_processing.process_weather_data(weather_data)

    return processed_data

The utils package contains two modules, api.py and data_processing.py, which contain helper functions to retrieve the raw weather data from an API and to process the raw data into a more readable format, respectively.

These modules can be reused across different projects, so it makes sense to organize them into a separate package.

# api.py
def get_weather_data(city: str) -> dict:
    """
    Retrieves the raw weather data for the given city.

    Args:
        city (str): The city for which to retrieve the weather data.

    Returns:
        dict: The raw weather data for the given city.
    """
    # code to retrieve data from API
    return raw_data

# data_processing.py
def process_weather_data(raw_data: dict) -> dict:
    """
    Processes the raw weather data into a more readable format.

    Args:
        raw_data (dict): The raw weather data.

    Returns:
        dict: The processed weather data.
    """
    # code to process data
    return processed_data

🧪 Test Your Code

Testing your code helps you catch bugs and ensure that your code works as expected.

Writing test cases is also an good way to document your code and help others understand it. Try all possible scenarios when testing your code, including edge cases and error conditions.

Consider a module calculator.py that implements a simple calculator with basic arithmetic operations. We can write test cases for each operation using a testing framework such as unittest.

import unittest
import calculator

class TestCalculator(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_addition(self):
        result = calculator.add(2, 3)
        self.assertEqual(result, 5)

    def test_subtraction(self):
        result = calculator.subtract(5, 3)
        self.assertEqual(result, 2)

    def test_multiplication(self):
        result = calculator.multiply(2, 3)
        self.assertEqual(result, 6)

    def test_division(self):
        result = calculator.divide(6, 2)
        self.assertEqual(result, 3)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

Each test case tests a single operation in the calculator module and uses the assertEqual method to verify that the result of the operation is as expected.

If any test fails, an error will be raised, and the test result will be reported as failed.

For debugging we can use the print statement to print the intermediate results or the values of variables in the code, or use a debugger such as pdb to step through the code and inspect the values of variables.

import calculator
import pdb

result = calculator.add(2, 3)
pdb.set_trace() # Set a breakpoint
print(result)

📜 Document Your Code

Documenting your code with docstrings can help others understand what it does and how it works.

Docstrings should provide a high-level overview of the code, including its purpose, usage, and limitations.

They should also be written in a clear and natural language style.

class Circle:
    """
    Class to represent a circle with a given radius.

    Attributes:
        radius (float): The radius of the circle.
    """

    def __init__(self, radius: float):
        """
        Initializes the Circle class with a given radius.

        Args:
            radius (float): The radius of the circle.
        """
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self) -> float:
        """
        Calculates the area of the circle.

        Returns:
            float: The area of the circle.
        """
        return 3.14 * (self.radius ** 2)

    def circumference(self) -> float:
        """
        Calculates the circumference of the circle.

        Returns:
            float: The circumference of the circle.
        """
        return 2 * 3.14 * self.radius

The class has a docstring explaining its purpose and the attributes it has.

Each method has its docstring explaining what it does and what arguments it takes and returns.

This makes the code easier to understand and maintain and more accessible for others to use and build upon.

💥 Handle Exceptions Gracefully

Handling exceptions in your code is essential for ensuring that it continues to run even when unexpected events occur.

Use try and except statements to handle exceptions and provide helpful error messages that explain what went wrong and how to fix it.

try:
    # code that may raise an exception
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError as error:
    # handle the exception
    print("An error occurred:", error)
    print("Please provide a non-zero value for division")

The code inside the try block may raise a ZeroDivisionError exception.

The except block handles the exception and prints a helpful error message to the user.

This way, the program can continue running even when an unexpected error occurs.

try:
    # code that may raise an exception
    with open("file.txt") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError as error:
    # handle the exception
    print("An error occurred:", error)
    print("Please provide a valid file path")
except Exception as error:
    # handle any other exceptions
    print("An unexpected error occurred:", error)

In this example, the code inside the try block may raise a FileNotFoundError or any other exception.

The first except block handles the FileNotFoundError and provides a helpful error message for the user.

The second except block handles any other exceptions that may occur and provides a generic error message.

This way the program can continue running even when unexpected errors occur and provide helpful error messages to the user.

🔑 Use Keyword Arguments

Keyword arguments are a powerful feature of Python that allows you to specify default values for function arguments and make your code more readable and flexible.

Using keyword arguments can also help you reduce the number of lines of code in your programs and make them easier to understand.

def greet(name, message="Hello"):
    print(f"{message}, {name}!")

greet("John") # Output: Hello, John!
greet("Jane", message="Hi") # Output: Hi, Jane!

In this example, the greet function takes in two arguments: name and message. The message argument has a default value of “Hello”.

When we call greet("John"), the default value of "Hello" is used for the message argument. But when we call greet("Jane", message="Hi"), the keyword argument is used instead, and the output is "Hi, Jane!".

🧘‍♀️ Follow the Zen of Python

The Zen of Python is a collection of principles and guidelines for writing good Python code.

It includes tips on writing simple, clear, and maintainable code and advice on choosing between different solutions.

import this

def sort_data(data):
    # Simple is better than complex
    data.sort()
    return data

# Readability counts
def add(a, b):
    # Explicit is better than implicit
    return a + b

# Flat is better than nested
def flatten(lists):
    result = []
    for sublist in lists:
        for item in sublist:
            result.append(item)
    return result

# Use meaningful names
def calculate_average_score(scores):
    total = 0
    count = 0
    for score in scores:
        total += score
        count += 1
    # One obvious way to do it
    return total / count

We follow the Zen of Python by:

  • Writing straightforward code (e.g. the sort_data function)
  • Choosing meaningful names for variables and functions (e.g. calculate_average_score)
  • Keeping the code flat and avoiding nested structures where possible (e.g. the flatten function)
  • Being explicit and transparent in our code (e.g. using return statements)

🛠 Refactor Your Code Regularly

Refactoring is improving the structure and quality of your code without changing its external behaviour.

It can help you identify areas that need improvement and make your code more maintainable over time. This can be especially important in projects with a long lifespan or requiring continuous updates.

So you can simplify complex sections, make your code more efficient, and eliminate any redundant or unnecessary parts. You can also take advantage of new features or libraries that have become available since you wrote the original code.

# Original code
def calculate_sum(numbers):
    result = 0
    for number in numbers:
        result += number
    return result

# Refactored code
def calculate_sum(numbers):
    return sum(numbers)

We have refactored the calculate_sum function to use the built-in sum function instead of manually iterating over the numbers and adding them up. This code is more efficient and readable and takes advantage of a built-in feature of Python that can perform the same calculation.
entry.summary: Let's look at the basic rules for writing great Python code
